facts.fact: It is the only industrial building Le Corbusier designed.
facts.quote: The building is the only industrial building designed by Le Corbusier.

facts.fact: In 2016 it joined UNESCO's World Heritage List with sixteen other Le Corbusier works, for its outstanding contribution to modern architecture.
facts.quote: In 2016, it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage along with sixteen other works by Le Corbusier, because of its outstanding contribution to the development of modern architecture.

facts.fact: Design studies began in January 1947, building started in April 1948 and was finished in 1951.
facts.quote: Studies began in January 1947 and construction began in early April 1948. Construction ended three years later in 1951.

facts.fact: It opened in 1952, its interior fitted with furniture by Charlotte Perriand and Jean Prouvé.
facts.quote: The factory opened in 1952 after its interior was fitted with furniture by Charlotte Perriand and Jean Prouvé.

facts.fact: The factory is built of reinforced concrete and raised on stilts.
facts.quote: The factory is built of reinforced concrete and mounted on stilts.

facts.fact: Le Corbusier's collaborators used it to test a full-size sunshade hung on the facade, meant both to look good and to cut direct light on workstations and protect delicate fabrics.
facts.quote: The project is also an opportunity for the architect's direct collaborators (Vladimir Bodiansky and André Wogenscky) to experiment with a life-size sunshade which, hung on the facade, would play both an aesthetic and functional role (reducing the diffusion direct light on workstations and protect fabrics with delicate colors).

facts.fact: Le Corbusier presented the roof terrace as an essential shared meeting place for the people who use a building, here a factory.
facts.quote: The “roof terrace” is presented by Le Corbusier as an essential place of conviviality between users of buildings, whether they are residential blocks, offices or, in this case, a factory.

facts.fact: Finished before the Unité in Marseille, it was the first building designed with the Modulor.
facts.quote: The manufacture, completed before the Unit of Marseille, is also the first building designed using the concept of Modulor.

facts.fact: A Roman Catholic church built on the Plateau d'Assy between 1937 and 1946, facing Mont Blanc.
facts.quote: The church of Notre-Dame de Toute Grâce du Plateau d'Assy (Our Lady Full of Grace of the Plateau d'Assy) is a Roman Catholic church in France, constructed on the plateau d'Assy between 1937 and 1946. It faces Mont Blanc, and is within the territory of the commune of Passy, in the Haute-Savoie department.

facts.fact: The young architect Maurice Novarina won the design contest held in 1937.
facts.quote: The contest took place in 1937 and was won by the young architect Maurice Novarina.

facts.fact: Working with Édouard Malot, Novarina built it of local Taveyannaz sandstone, the stone used for Savoie chalets.
facts.quote: In collaboration with Édouard Malot, Novarina designed a church to be built out of local stone, called Taveyannaz sandstone; it is the same type of stone frequently used to build chalets in the Savoie.

facts.fact: Its pointed roof is made to carry heavy snow.
facts.quote: The roof is pointed and is meant to sustain large amounts of snow; the foundation of the structure is solidly anchored in the soil.

facts.fact: A 28-metre bell tower, designed to withstand local earth movements, tops the church.
facts.quote: The church is topped by a massive twenty-eight-metre bell tower, carefully designed to withstand local tectonic movements.

facts.fact: Inside, a rectangular nave with two aisles leads to a semicircular choir with an ambulatory, set above the crypt.
facts.quote: The interior of the building is meant to resemble a Roman chapel, with a rectangular nave flanked by two aisles. The choir is semicircular, surrounded by an ambulatory and sitting above the crypt.

facts.fact: Its interior was decorated by leading artists of the time, among them Bonnard, Léger, Lurçat, Richier, Rouault, Matisse, Braque, Lipchitz and Chagall.
facts.quote: Among those who contributed paintings, sculptures, tapestries, stained glass, ceramics, and mosaics to the church were Pierre Bonnard, Fernand Léger, Jean Lurçat, his student Paul Cosandier, Germaine Richier, Georges Rouault, Jean Bazaine, Henri Matisse, Georges Braque, Jacques Lipchitz, Marc Chagall, Constant Demaison, Ladislas Kijno, Claude Mary, Carlo Sergio Signori, and Théodore Strawinsky.

facts.fact: It was listed as a monument historique on 11 June 2004.
facts.quote: On June 11, 2004, Notre-Dame de Toute Grâce du Plateau d'Assy was classed as a monument historique de France.

facts.fact: A railway arch bridge over the Truyère near Ruynes-en-Margeride, in France's Massif Central.
facts.quote: The Garabit viaduct (French: viaduc de Garabit) is a railway arch bridge spanning the Truyère, near Ruynes-en-Margeride, Cantal, France, in the mountainous Massif Central region.

facts.fact: Gustave Eiffel built it in 1882–1884, with structural engineering by Maurice Koechlin; it is 565 m long with a main arch spanning 165 m.
facts.quote: The bridge was constructed between 1882 and 1884 by Gustave Eiffel, with structural engineering by Maurice Koechlin, and was opened in 1885. It is 565 m (1,854 ft) in length and has a principal arch of 165 m (541 ft) span.

facts.fact: A parabolic arch carries a single rail line across the gorge; it opened in November 1885.
facts.quote: The Garabit viaduct, which uses a parabolic arch to support a single rail line across the gorge, opened in November 1885.

facts.fact: Standing 124 m above the river, it had the world's longest arch when completed in 1884.
facts.quote: The bridge, which is 124 m (407 ft) above the river, had the world's longest arch when it was completed in 1884.

facts.fact: Trains deflect it by about 8 mm, the same figure Eiffel calculated.
facts.quote: Rail traffic using the bridge causes a deflection (load displacement) of about 8 millimetres (0.315 in), which was the same value as the one calculated by Eiffel.

facts.fact: After Eiffel's firm built the Maria Pia Bridge in Porto, the Garabit job was given to Eiffel without the usual competitive tender.
facts.quote: Between 1875 and 1877, the company had built the Maria Pia Bridge over the Douro at Porto, and when the construction of a railway between Marvejols and Neussargues, both in Cantal, was proposed, the work of constructing a viaduct to cross the Truyère was given to Eiffel without the usual process of competitive tendering.

facts.fact: The crossing weighs 3,587 tonnes.
facts.quote: The crossing is 565 m (1,854 ft) long and weighs (metric) 3,587 tonnes (3,530 long tons; 3,954 short tons).

facts.fact: A public cultural centre in Paris's 19th arrondissement, opened on 11 October 2008 in the former municipal undertaker's at 104 rue d'Aubervilliers.
facts.quote: The Cent Quatre (pronounced [sɑ̃ katʁ], meaning "104") is a public cultural centre in Paris, which opened on 11 October 2008 on the site of a former municipal undertaker's at 104 rue d'Aubervilliers, in the 19th arrondissement of the city.

facts.fact: The original building opened in 1874, designed by Édouard Delebarre de Bay and Godon under the supervision of Victor Baltard, chief architect of Paris.
facts.quote: In 1874, after two years of work, the building was inaugurated. It was the work of the architects Édouard Delebarre de Bay and Godon, under the supervision of Victor Baltard, chief architect of Paris.

facts.fact: It was built like the train stations and exhibition halls of its day, around a cast-iron frame with glass and brick.
facts.quote: The building was conceived in the style of the industrial architecture of the time (that of large train stations and exhibition halls), and constructed around a cast-iron frame using glass and brick.

facts.fact: It had two large canopied halls, loading bays, stables and cellars, and was over 270 m long.
facts.quote: The surface area of the building was the same as the Place de la République. It consisted of two large canopied halls, loading bays, areas, stables and cellars, and was over 270 m (890 ft) long.

facts.fact: For over 120 years it housed the Paris city undertakers, with over 1,000 staff organising 150 funeral processions a day.
facts.quote: For over 120 years, the building housed the city undertakers for Paris. Over 1,000 people worked in the building, organising 150 funeral processions per day.

facts.fact: It has been a registered historic monument since 21 January 1997.
facts.quote: The building has been registered as a historic monument since 21 January 1997.

facts.fact: In 2003 the city chose the Paris architects Atelier Novembre for the conversion, judging their proposal best at respecting the site's character.
facts.quote: In 2003 the city administration awarded the contract for the redevelopment of the site to the Paris-based architects Atelier Novembre, following a tendering process. Their proposal was judged as best respecting the character of the site.

facts.fact: The old basement stables became event and exhibition space.
facts.quote: The former stables in the basement have been renovated as event and exhibition space.

facts.fact: In the late 1920s the council under mayor André Morizet decided on a larger town hall, sited on a former quarry.
facts.quote: In the late 1920s, the town council, led by the mayor, André Morizet, decided to commission a more substantial town hall in the centre of the Boulogne-Billancourt conurbation. The site they selected was a former quarry at the corner of Rue Gallieni and Rue Paul-Bert.

facts.fact: Building began in December 1931.
facts.quote: Construction of the new building started in December 1931.

facts.fact: Tony Garnier and Jacques Debat-Ponsan designed it in the Art Deco style in reinforced concrete; it opened on 15 December 1934.
facts.quote: It was designed by Tony Garnier and Jacques Debat-Ponsan in the Art Deco style, built in reinforced concrete and was officially opened by Morizet on 15 December 1934.

facts.fact: The plan has two rectangular blocks, the rear one taller and wider than the front.
facts.quote: The layout involved two rectangular blocks with the rear block taller and wider than the front block.

facts.fact: The front block has a symmetrical 19-bay main facade.
facts.quote: The design of the front block involved a symmetrical main frontage of 19 bays facing onto the main road (now Avenue André Morizet).

facts.fact: A short flight of steps in the central bay leads to a deeply recessed doorway under a curved canopy.
facts.quote: The central bay featured a short flight of steps leading up to a heavily recessed doorway with a curved canopy.

facts.fact: The main room, the Grand Hall des Guichets in the rear block, is 65 m long and 28 m wide.
facts.quote: Internally the principal room was the Grand Hall des Guichets (the large ticket hall), which was 65 meters (213 ft) long and 28 metres (92 ft) wide, and was accommodated in the rear block.

facts.fact: It was listed as a monument historique in 1975.
facts.quote: The Hôtel de Ville (French pronunciation: [otɛl də vil], City Hall) is a municipal building in Boulogne-Billancourt, Hauts-de-Seine, in the western suburbs of Paris, France standing on Avenue André Morizet. It was designated a monument historique by the French government in 1975.

facts.fact: A French art school, contemporary art centre and research institution in Nice.
facts.quote: The Villa Arson, also referred to as the École Nationale Supérieure d'Arts à la Villa Arson (National School of Fine Arts at the Villa Arson), is a French art museum, elite school and research institution for contemporary art, located in Nice, France.

facts.fact: In 1965 Nice gave the school the former Arson family home; Michel Marot's expansion into an international fine art school was completed in 1970.
facts.quote: In 1965, the city of Nice offered the former home of the Arson family to the school; and an expansion of the two acre property to create an international fine art school, designed by Michel Marot, is completed in 1970.

facts.fact: The Villa Arson was Michel Marot's most famous project.
facts.quote: In 1970, he designed his most famous project, the Villa Arson in Nice.

facts.fact: It sits on a hill in Saint Barthélemy, in the north of Nice, and covers 23,000 m2.
facts.quote: La Villa Arson is located on a hill in the neighbourhood of Saint Barthélemy, in the northern district of the city of Nice, and occupies a vast area of 23,000 m2.

facts.fact: The site overlooks the city and the Riviera coast, and its many courtyards, terraces and gardens make the most of the view, planting and daylight.
facts.quote: The site overlooks the city and the coastline of the French Riviera and is designed to emphasis its view, as-well-as vegetation and natural light, with the wide use of courtyards, terraces and gardens.

facts.fact: The school and the new national contemporary art centre were inaugurated together as the Villa Arson in 1972.
facts.quote: The Centre Nationale d'Art Contemporain was established in 1971, and the École and the Centre were officially inaugurated under the name "la Villa Arson" in 1972 by then Minister of Cultural Affairs, Jacques Duhamel.

facts.fact: Italy's busiest railway station, used by about 150 million passengers a year.
facts.quote: It is Italy's busiest railway station and the fifth-busiest in Europe, with a traffic volume of approximately 150 million passengers per year, and with 850 trains in transit per day.

facts.fact: Two teams chosen in a 1947 competition designed it, Leo Calini and Eugenio Montuori, and Castellazzi, Fadigati, Pintonello and Vitellozzi; it opened in 1950.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the two teams selected through a competition in 1947: Leo Calini and Eugenio Montuori; Massimo Castellazzi, Vasco Fadigati, Achille Pintonello and Annibale Vitellozzi. It was inaugurated in 1950.

facts.fact: The great hall has full-height glass walls and a concrete roof shaped as a flattened, segmented arch, a modern take on a Roman bath's barrel vault.
facts.quote: This great hall is fronted by full-height glass walls, and is covered by a concrete roof that consists of a flattened and segmented arch, a modernist version of a barrel vault from a Roman bath.

facts.fact: The vault is built as one structure with a cantilevered canopy over the entrance drive.
facts.quote: The vault is structurally integrated with a cantilevered canopy that extends over the entrance drive.

facts.fact: Behind the hall, a longer travertine-clad block holds a 10-storey hotel.
facts.quote: The back of the hall leads to a transition space of ticketing functions and shops before reaching the train shed, and is topped by an even longer building block that houses a 10-story hotel, clad with travertine.

facts.fact: The anodised aluminium frieze along the glass wall is by Amerigo Tot and evokes the sound and speed of a train.
facts.quote: The anodized aluminium frieze panels set in sequence along the length of the glass wall are the work of Hungarian-Italian artist Amerigo Tot. The composition relates to the theme of capturing the dynamics of sound and speed of a train.

facts.fact: Side wings from Angiolo Mazzoni's earlier, unfinished design are part of today's station.
facts.quote: The side structures of the design by Angiolo Mazzoni form part of the present-day station.

facts.fact: A stretch of Rome's 4th-century BC Servian Wall survives outside the station.
facts.quote: A length of the early 4th century BC Roman Servian Wall is preserved outside the station.

facts.fact: It was designed in the 1920s as the training ground for the Fascist Academy of Physical Education, now the seat of Italy's Olympic Committee.
facts.quote: Stadio dei Marmi was designed in the 1920s as a complement to the annex Fascist Academy of Physical Education (now the seat of CONI, Italian Olympic Committee), to be used by its students for training.

facts.fact: Designed by Enrico Del Debbio, it opened in 1932 near Monte Mario, under Mussolini.
facts.quote: The Stadio dei Marmi first opened in 1932, on the 10th anniversary of the March on Rome, near the Roman neighborhood Monte Mario, by the architect Enrico Del Debbio under the Fascist ruler Benito Mussolini.

facts.fact: Sixty 4-metre classical statues of athletes in Carrara marble ring the stadium.
facts.quote: The Stadio dei Marmi is encircled by sixty, 4-meter tall classical statues of athletes made from Carrara marble.

facts.fact: The statues were gifts from Italy's provinces and were made by twenty-four sculptors chosen by contest.
facts.quote: The sixty towering Carrara marble athletic statues ringing the stadium were gifted by the Italian provinces and embodied the ancient cardinal Roman values: virilitas, fortitudo, disciplina, and gravitas (virility, fortitude, discipline, and dignity). They were designed and produced by twenty-four sculptors, who were chosen from a contest, and included artists like Nicola D'Antino, Aldo Buttini, Silvio Canevari, Carlo de Veroli, Publio Morbiducci, Eugenio Baroni, Arnolfo Bellini, Francesco Messina, and Romano Romanelli.

facts.fact: Modelled on Greek and Roman statues, they stand out against the stadium's plain white marble architecture.
facts.quote: The sculptors adhered to classical forms and elements, when they used Greek and Roman statues as models, such as Doryphoros of Polykleitos and Discobolus of Myron, which stood out against the plain white marble architecture of the stadium.

facts.fact: Del Debbio described the sports complex as an architecture of severe monumentality that harks back to the monuments of ancient Rome.
facts.quote: According to the architect Enrico Del Debbio, the sports complex was designed as an "architectonic complex of severe monumentality ... the result is the emergence of a monumental group, which can be traced back to the greatest monuments of ancient Rome."

facts.fact: It was built to celebrate the Fascist regime and its youth movement.
facts.quote: The stadium was built to celebrate Fascist accomplishments and the Gioventú del Littorio, the youth movement of the National Fascist Party of Italy.

facts.fact: It hosted field hockey preliminaries at the 1960 Summer Olympics.
facts.quote: Subsequently the Stadio dei Marmi has been used to host some of the field hockey preliminaries for the 1960 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: A house museum in Milan, built in 1932–1935 as a single-family house by the Rationalist architect Piero Portaluppi, in a large garden with a tennis court and pool.
facts.quote: Villa Necchi Campiglio is a historic residence (house museum) located at via Mozart, 14, Milan. It was built between 1932 and 1935 as an independent single-family house designed by Piero Portaluppi, an important Milanese Rationalist architect, and is surrounded by a large private garden with a tennis court and swimming pool.

facts.fact: Its pool was the second built in Milan and the first on private land.
facts.quote: This was the second swimming pool ever to be built in Milan after the municipal one, and the first to be built on private land.

facts.fact: It was meant to be modern in style and services, with a lift, dumbwaiter, intercoms, telephones and a heated pool.
facts.quote: The house was envisioned as an elegant yet comfortable dwelling, modern in both style and facilities, as evidenced by the inclusion of an elevator, a dumbwaiter, intercoms and telephones, and a heated swimming pool.

facts.fact: From 1938 Tomaso Buzzi remodelled the exterior and some rooms in a softer, 18th-century-inspired style, unlike Portaluppi's original minimalism.
facts.quote: Beginning in 1938, and for the next twenty years, the Necchi Campiglio family engaged architect Tomaso Buzzi to redesign the exterior and subsequently the furnishings of some rooms in a style inspired by 18th-century art, which was softer and more elaborate compared to the original minimalism of Portaluppi's spaces.

facts.fact: The sisters, without heirs, left the house to FAI, the Italian Environmental Fund.
facts.quote: Without heirs, the sisters were concerned with finding a suitable purpose for the house, ultimately bequeathing it to FAI (Italian Environmental Fund).

facts.fact: Restoration took over three years and about six million euros; the villa opened to the public in May 2008.
facts.quote: The works required over three years and an expenditure of approximately six million Euros. Upon completion, the villa was opened to the public in May 2008.

facts.fact: Luca Guadagnino's film I Am Love was shot at the villa in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, Luca Guadagnino's film I Am Love was filmed at the villa.

facts.fact: A skyscraper in Milan's Centro Direzionale business district, designed by Melchiorre Bega in 1956 and completed in 1959.
facts.quote: The Galfa Building or Galfa Tower (Torre Galfa in Italian) is a skyscraper in Milan, Italy, located in the Centro Direzionale di Milano district, north of the city centre. It was designed by architect Melchiorre Bega in 1956 and completed in 1959.

facts.fact: Its name joins the two streets it faces, Via Galvani and Via Fara.
facts.quote: The name "Galfa" is a portmanteau derived from the names of the two streets where the tower has its facades, Via Galvani and Via Fara.

facts.fact: It is 109 m tall with 31 floors above ground and 2 below.
facts.quote: The building is 109 m and 31 floors high, with 2 more underground floors, and qualifies as the eleventh highest skyscraper in Milan.

facts.fact: The design follows the International Style.
facts.quote: The overall design of the tower is mainly based on the International Style architecture.

facts.fact: The plan is rectangular, with the two lowest floors wider than the tower; its reinforced-concrete frame is almost entirely hidden behind glass and aluminium curtain walls.
facts.quote: The building is rectangular, with the two lowest floors larger than the main body. The main structure in reinforced concrete is almost completely hidden by curtain walls made of glass and aluminium.

facts.fact: Built for the Sarom company, it was sold in the mid-1970s to the Popolare di Milano bank, which used it as a headquarters.
facts.quote: The tower was originally built for the Sarom company; in the mid-1970s, it was sold by Sarom to the Popolare di Milano bank, and thereafter served as a service centre and headquarter of the bank.

facts.fact: In May 2012 a group occupied the empty tower to make a space for artists, a project called Macao.
facts.quote: On 5 May 2012, the building was occupied by a group of people which intended to create a space for artists; the project's name was Macao.

facts.fact: Renovation led by Studio BG&K began in 2016, planned to give it a mix of homes, hotel and shops.
facts.quote: Work began in 2016, led by the design firm, Studio BG&K. In an interview with the Italian design magazine Abitare, Maurice Kanah, lead architect on the project, said that the refurbished building will contain "a mix of residential, hotel and commercial functions.”

facts.fact: A former Fiat car factory on Via Nizza in Turin, now Fiat's head office and a multipurpose centre designed by Renzo Piano.
facts.quote: Lingotto is a building complex on Via Nizza in Turin, Italy. It once housed a car factory built by Italian automotive company Fiat and today houses the administrative headquarters of the manufacturer and a multipurpose centre projected by architect Renzo Piano.

facts.fact: Built 1916–1923 to a design by the young Giacomo Matté-Trucco, it had five floors: raw materials came in at the bottom and cars were built on a line rising up through the building.
facts.quote: In 1916, construction started on the complex, and it was completed in 1923. The design by the young architect Giacomo Matté-Trucco was unusual in that it had five floors, with raw materials going in at the ground floor, and cars built on a line that went up through the building.

facts.fact: Finished cars came out on the roof onto a 1.5 km test track, with spiral concrete ramps at each end.
facts.quote: Finished cars emerged at rooftop level to go onto a 1,500-metre (1.5 km; 4,900 ft; 0.93 mi) long test track, with spiral concrete access ramps at each end.

facts.fact: Built by G A Porcheddu's company, it was the world's largest car factory at the time.
facts.quote: The construction was carried out by the company of G A Porcheddu. It was the largest car factory in the world at that time.

facts.fact: Le Corbusier called it one of the most impressive sights in industry.
facts.quote: For its time, the Lingotto building was avant garde, influential, and impressive—Le Corbusier called it "one of the most impressive sights in industry", and "a guideline for town planning".

facts.fact: Overtaken by the larger Mirafiori plant, the factory closed in 1982.
facts.quote: By the late 1970s, the factory had become obsolete — having been superseded by the larger and more advanced Fiat Mirafiori factory — and a decision was made to finally close it in 1982.

facts.fact: Renzo Piano won the competition to convert it into concert halls, a theatre, a convention centre, shops and a hotel.
facts.quote: An architectural competition was held, which was eventually awarded to Renzo Piano, who envisioned an exciting public space for the city. The old factory was restored into a modern complex, with concert halls, theatre, a convention centre, shopping arcades, and a hotel.

facts.fact: The rooftop test track was kept and can still be visited.
facts.quote: The track was retained, and can still be visited today on the top floor of the shopping mall and hotel.

facts.fact: A Roman Catholic titular parish church on Piazza Santa Maria Consolatrice in Rome's Tiburtino district.
facts.quote: St. Mary the Consoler at Tiburtino (Italian: Santa Maria Consolatrice al Tiburtino) is a Roman Catholic titular parish church in Rome. It is located in Piazza Santa Maria Consolatrice, within the quartiere Tiburtino.

facts.fact: Designed in 1935 and finished in 1959, it has housed Italy's Ministry of Foreign Affairs since completion.
facts.quote: The Palazzo della Farnesina is an Italian government building located between Monte Mario and the Tiber River in the Foro Italico area in Rome, Italy. Designed in 1935, it has housed the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs since its completion in 1959.

facts.fact: Enrico Del Debbio, Arnaldo Foschini and Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo designed the nine-storey building as headquarters of the National Fascist Party.
facts.quote: The nine-story building was designed in 1935 by architects Enrico Del Debbio, Arnaldo Foschini and Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo. It was originally designated to be the headquarters of Italy's National Fascist Party.

facts.fact: Construction stopped in 1943 and through the Second World War.
facts.quote: Construction was halted in 1943 and throughout World War II.

facts.fact: The facade is travertine.
facts.quote: The facade consists of travertine.

facts.fact: It has over 1,300 rooms, is 169 m wide and 51 m tall, and is one of the largest buildings in Italy.
facts.quote: The building consists of more than 1,300 rooms, is 169 meters in width, 51 meters tall, with a total area of 120,000 square meters and has a total internal volume of approximately 720,000 cubic meters. It is comparable in size to the Caserta Palace and is one of the largest buildings in Italy.

facts.fact: Finished close to its original design, it brought together the ministry's 13 separate offices.
facts.quote: The Palazzo della Farnesina was completed in 1959, varying only slightly from its original design. Upon completion, it consolidated the 13 separate offices of the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

facts.fact: Its name comes from the Farnese Gardens, land once owned by Pope Paul III (Alessandro Farnese).
facts.quote: Its name comes from the land on which it rises, the area between Monte Mario and the Tiber, which were called the Farnese Gardens (Orti della Farnesina) due to the ownership of Pope Paul III who was originally named Alessandro Farnese.

facts.fact: The home of the Venice Film Festival, on the Lido.
facts.quote: Palazzo del Cinema di Venezia is the place that hosts the Venice Film Festival and congress activities, located in Lido di Venezia, Venice, Italy.

facts.fact: The festival began in 1932 on a hotel terrace; its own building followed in 1936–1937, designed by the engineer Luigi Quagliata in a modernist spirit.
facts.quote: The first cinema exhibition was held on the terrace of the Hotel Excelsior on August 6, 1932. But, with the growing success, it became necessary to build a proper and prestigious venue; this took place between 1936 and 1937, based on a project by the engineer Luigi Quagliata, faithful to the dictates of modernism.

facts.fact: The plan set three rationalist buildings symmetrically, with the Casino in the centre and the cinema on the left; the third, an ice rink, was never built because of the war.
facts.quote: The urban plan envisaged the symmetrical construction of three buildings in the rationalist style, with the Casino in the center, the cinema building on the left and a third mirror building on the right, intended to house an ice skating rink, which was not built due to the onset of the Second World War.

facts.fact: It opened on 10 August 1937 with a simple hall and a thousand-seat cinema, today's Great Hall.
facts.quote: The Palazzo del Cinema, inaugurated on 10 August 1937 for the fifth edition of the Exhibition was then made up of a simple hall and a thousand-seat cinema hall (the present Great Hall).

facts.fact: Quagliata planned an expansion in 1952, but only the forepart and the open-air arena were built.
facts.quote: Following the continuous success of the festival, it became necessary to expand the building, which was entrusted to Quagliata himself in 1952. The overall project included the expansion of the Great Hall, an open arena, other cinemas, offices and services.; but only the forepart and the uncovered arena were built.

facts.fact: It has three cinemas: the Sala Grande with over 1,000 seats, the Zorzi and the Pasinetti.
facts.quote: There are three theaters in Palazzo del cinema: la Sala Grande with over 1 032 seats, the Zorzi (48 seats) and Pasinetti (119 seats) theatres.

facts.fact: A cultural foundation in Venice set up in 1869 by the last Querini Stampalia, Count Giovanni Querini; Carlo Scarpa designed the ground-floor interiors, exterior elements and garden of its historic palazzo.
facts.quote: The Fondazione Querini Stampalia is a cultural institution in Venice, Italy, founded in 1869 at the behest of the last descendant of the Venetian Querini Stampalia family, Conte Giovanni Querini (Count John Querini). Architect Carlo Scarpa designed interior, exterior, and garden elements and spaces on the ground floor of the historic building.

facts.fact: Scarpa's work there dates from 1961–1963.
facts.quote: Fondazione Querini Stampalia, Venice, 1961–1963

facts.fact: The foundation's director when Scarpa completed his renovation and garden was Giuseppe Mazzariol.
facts.quote: Scarpa was Mario Botta's thesis adviser along with Giuseppe Mazzariol; the latter was the director of the Fondazione Querini Stampalia when Scarpa completed his renovation and garden for that institution.

facts.fact: The Palazzo Querini Stampalia holds living quarters, an archive, a library and a museum of paintings and furnishings.
facts.quote: The foundation is located in the Palazzo Querini Stampalia and includes living quarters, an archive, a library, and a museum of paintings and furnishings, the Pinacoteca Querini Stampalia.

facts.fact: It stands just south of the church of Santa Maria Formosa in Castello.
facts.quote: Located just South of the Church of Santa Maria Formosa in the sestiere Castello, the Foundation is open to the public for academic research.

facts.fact: Its library opens even on Sundays and is considered one of the most beautiful public libraries in Venice.
facts.quote: The Biblioteca della Fondazione Querini Stampalia, the Foundation Library, is open even on Sundays, the only one of its kind in the city, from 10 AM to 7 PM. It is considered to be one of the most beautiful public libraries in the city.

facts.fact: Scarpa was shaped by the materials, landscape and history of Venice, and by Japan.
facts.quote: Carlo Scarpa (2 June 1906 – 28 November 1978) was an Italian architect and designer. He was influenced by the materials, landscape, and history of Venetian culture, as well as those of Japan.

facts.fact: Seating over 70,000, it is Rome's largest sports venue and the second-largest in Italy after San Siro.
facts.quote: Seating over 70,000 spectators, it is the largest sports facility in Rome and the second-largest in Italy, after Milan's San Siro.

facts.fact: It stands in the Foro Italico; building began in 1928 under Enrico Del Debbio and Luigi Moretti expanded it in 1937.
facts.quote: The Olimpico is located in northwestern Rome in the Foro Italico sports complex. Construction began in 1928 under Enrico Del Debbio and the venue was expanded in 1937 by Luigi Moretti.

facts.fact: Annibale Vitellozzi took over the post-war rebuild in 1951 after Carlo Roccatelli died, and it was finished in 1952.
facts.quote: Annibale Vitellozzi replaced Roccatelli in 1951 after the latter's death. In 1952, the stadium's reconstruction was completed, at a cost of 3,400,000,000 lire (approx 1,700,000 €).

facts.fact: The rebuilt stadium was a 33,500 m2 concrete structure clad in travertine.
facts.quote: The new stadium was a 33,500 square-metre concrete structure, clad with travertine.

facts.fact: The pitch was sunk below ground so the stadium would not dominate the Foro Italico's skyline.
facts.quote: The sinking of the pitch was done to prevent the stadium from dominating the Foro Italico's skyline, and to match with other buildings.

facts.fact: It opened on 17 May 1953 as the Stadio dei Centomila, the stadium of the 100,000.
facts.quote: The Stadio dei Centomila (Stadium of the 100,000), named after its expected capacity, was officially opened on 17 May 1953 by the President of Italy, Luigi Einaudi.

facts.fact: It was rebuilt and roofed for the 1990 FIFA World Cup.
facts.quote: In 1990, the Olimpico was rebuilt and roofed for the 1990 FIFA World Cup.

facts.fact: The roof is a Teflon and fibreglass membrane hung from 88 steel radial cables between an outer steel ring on 12 steel pillars and an inner ring.
facts.quote: The roof consists of a 13-metre-high (43 ft) outer steel ring which is 29 metres (95 ft) above the ground on 12 steel pillars and four external concrete stair blocks which are also pillars; radial bearing and stabilizing cables hold an inner steel ring. The roof itself is a Teflon and fiberglass membrane which is hung from the 88 steel radial cables linking the external and internal rings.

facts.fact: The fourth bridge over Venice's Grand Canal, designed by Santiago Calatrava.
facts.quote: The Ponte della Costituzione (English: Constitution Bridge) is the fourth bridge over the Grand Canal in Venice, Italy. It was designed by Santiago Calatrava, and was moved into place in 2007 (connecting Stazione di Santa Lucia to Piazzale Roma), amid protest by politicians and the general public.

facts.fact: Commissioned in 1999, Calatrava proposed a wide-radius arch built off-site and installed entirely from the canal.
facts.quote: Using a public selection process, they commissioned Santiago Calatrava in November 1999 to design the new bridge. Calatrava's response was an arched bridge with a large radius which was designed to be constructed off-site and installed entirely from the canal.

facts.fact: It links the Santa Lucia railway station with Piazzale Roma, where visitors arrive by car and bus.
facts.quote: The bridge is situated at a strategic point, connecting the railway station (Stazione Santa Lucia), on the north with the Piazzale Roma (the City's arrival point by car/bus), on the south side of the Grand Canal.

facts.fact: It is an arched truss bridge with a 180 m radius: a central arch, two side arches and two lower arches, tied together by cross girders.
facts.quote: Calatrava designed an arched truss bridge with a radius of 180 metres (590 ft), with a central arch, two side arches and two lower arches. Girders placed perpendicular to the arches join them together.

facts.fact: The steps alternate Istrian stone with lit tempered glass; the glass parapet ends in a bronze handrail with hidden lighting.
facts.quote: The stairway on the bridge is paved with pietra d'Istria, a stone traditionally used in Venice, alternating with tempered glass steps illuminated from below by fluorescent lights. The parapet is also tempered glass, terminating in a bronze handrail with concealed lighting.

facts.fact: After being built off-site, it was moved into place by a large barge in July 2007.
facts.quote: After fabrication, the bridge was moved into place by a large barge in July 2007.

facts.fact: Critics objected to its lack of wheelchair access, its necessity and its modern style in medieval Venice.
facts.quote: The bridge has received heated criticism and seen inauguration delays and walk-outs, which originated from three main grievances: the lack of wheelchair access, the lack of its necessity and its modernist-minimalist style being incompatible with Venice's decorative medieval architecture.

facts.fact: In 2022 the city decided to replace all the slippery glass sections with trachyte stone.
facts.quote: In 2022, safety concerns overcame aesthetic principles when the city determined to replace all the glass sections with trachyte stone, to prevent regularly occurring falls.

facts.fact: Rome's second-largest railway station after Termini.
facts.quote: Roma Tiburtina is the second largest railway station in Rome, after Roma Termini.

facts.fact: The station first opened in 1866.
facts.quote: Roma Tiburtina originally opened in 1866, only three years after the first (temporary) Roma Termini.

facts.fact: The redeveloped station was designed by Paolo Desideri.
facts.quote: The redeveloped station was designed by architect Paolo Desideri, while the responsibility for managing both the design and construction phases resided with the Gemmo Railway Division, which also administered electrical and mechanical systems as well as the project's technical and financial aspects.

facts.fact: It is a large bridge over the tracks linking the Nomentano and Pietralata districts: a glazed box 240 m long and 50 m wide, raised 9 m above the ground.
facts.quote: As designed, the new Roma Tiburtina takes the form of a large bridge spanning across the railway lines and connecting between the Nomentano and Pietralata districts. It is an enclosed glazed parallelepiped structure, with a length of 240 metres (790 ft), a width of 50 m (160 ft), and suspended 9 m (30 ft) above ground level.

facts.fact: Inside, eight separate rooms hang from the roof, which helps isolate them from train noise and vibration.
facts.quote: The interior space is divided into eight separate rooms suspended from the roof. The suspension of the main structure offers several advantages, including a greater level of isolation from the noise and vibration generated by the passage of trains beneath it.

facts.fact: 29 escalators and 52 lifts connect the platforms with the rooms above.
facts.quote: The ground level platforms are connected to the suspended rooms above via an assortment of 29 escalators and 52 elevators.

facts.fact: It opened on 28 November 2011, dedicated to Cavour, at a cost of about €330 million, almost double the estimate.
facts.quote: On 28 November 2011, following three years of construction work, the new station was officially inaugurated and dedicated to Cavour. By the end of the project, the total construction costs had almost doubled from the original projected figure to around €330 million.

facts.fact: Building it took about 13,400 tonnes of steel and 95,000 m3 of concrete.
facts.quote: Roughly 13,400 tonnes (13,200 long tons; 14,800 short tons) of steel and 95,000 cubic metres (124,000 yd3) of concrete was used during the station's construction.

facts.fact: A skyscraper in Turin and the headquarters of the Intesa Sanpaolo banking group.
facts.quote: Grattacielo Intesa Sanpaolo in Turin, Italy is a skyscraper as well as the headquarters for the banking group Intesa Sanpaolo.

facts.fact: It is Turin's third-tallest building and holds offices for more than 2,000 staff plus facilities open to the public.
facts.quote: The building is the third tallest in the city, after the landmark Mole Antonelliana which has held the record since 1889, and Piedmont Region Headquarters. It provides office accommodation for more than 2,000 employees as well as providing leisure facilities for the general public.

facts.fact: A rooftop greenhouse holds Piano35, a public restaurant, with a roof garden and a panoramic terrace.
facts.quote: At its summit, a rooftop greenhouse houses Piano35, a public restaurant, alongside a roof garden and a panoramic terrace that provides far-reaching views over the city.

facts.fact: At its base a 364-seat public hall hangs from transfer trusses four storeys above the ground.
facts.quote: At its base, a 364-seat multifunctional public hall/auditorium is hung from the transfer trusses four stories above ground level.

facts.fact: Renzo Piano called it a bioclimatic building: naturally ventilated and cooled, with much of its power from photovoltaic panels on the south facade.
facts.quote: Renzo Piano, Grattacielo Intesa Sanpaolo's architect, described the skyscraper as a "bioclimatic building", being naturally ventilated and cooled; with a substantial amount of its power requirement to be generated from photovoltaic panels that cover the southern façade.

facts.fact: It received a LEED Platinum rating, the only high-rise in Europe to hold one.
facts.quote: Renzo Piano, Grattacielo Intesa Sanpaolo's architect, described the skyscraper as a "bioclimatic building", being naturally ventilated and cooled; with a substantial amount of its power requirement to be generated from photovoltaic panels that cover the southern façade. It was awarded the LEED Platinum rating, making it the only high-rise building in Europe to hold such a certification.

facts.fact: After disputes over its height and effect on the skyline, construction began in December 2008.
facts.quote: After controversies on its height and the impact on the skyline, construction eventually started in December 2008.

facts.fact: Completed in December 2014, it won ArchDaily readers' Building of the Year award for offices in 2016.
facts.quote: In December 2014, construction was completed and the first 50 employees of the Bank moved in the new premises. In 2016, readers of ArchDaily magazine voted the tower winner of the Building of the Year award, in the office category.

facts.fact: A high-speed railway station near Naples, in Afragola, inaugurated on 6 June 2017.
facts.quote: Naples Afragola (Italian: Stazione di Napoli Afragola) is a railway station near Naples that was inaugurated on 6 June 2017, with regular traffic for passengers starting from 11 June 2017.

facts.fact: Zaha Hadid Architects won the design contract in 2003; the design was presented that November, with opening then planned for 2009.
facts.quote: In 2003, a contract was awarded to architect Zaha Hadid Architects for the station design. On 4 November 2003, Zaha Hadid formally presented the design, then projected to open in 2009.

facts.fact: The building is a bridge over its four tracks, four levels and up to 25 m high, holding a 20,000 m2 concourse.
facts.quote: From its inception the building was envisioned as a bridge over its four tracks, with four levels and a maximum height of 25 metres (82 ft). Accommodating the station's concourse, the bridge has an area of 20,000 square metres (220,000 sq ft), as well as provision for an additional 10,000 square metres (110,000 sq ft).

facts.fact: Putting the concourse directly above the platforms shortens walks and favours neither side of the line.
facts.quote: Placing the concourse directly above each platform minimizes passenger walking, without prioritizing the communities at one end of the station over the other.

facts.fact: Large glass panels form winding shapes on the outside, said to evoke a moving train.
facts.quote: The exterior features large glass panels forming winding shapes, described as evoking a moving train.

facts.fact: For earthquakes, the building is split into zones no longer than 50 m that can move separately.
facts.quote: The design addressed seismic requirements by dividing the building into zones no greater in length than 50 m (160 ft); enabling the sections to move individually in a seismic event.

facts.fact: The glazed roof has internal shading and acoustic baffles that cut sun and glare, and vents that let out heat so the concourse is naturally ventilated most of the time.
facts.quote: One major example of this design attention is the glazed roof, which features internal shading and acoustic baffles, limiting the amount of direct sunlight and glare on the concourse as well directing excess heat away via purpose-built roof vents; this enabled natural ventilation practices to be used under normal conditions.

facts.fact: Its curved structural parts were mainly concrete, shaped with prefabricated steel units and CNC-milled moulds, using techniques the architects had used before.
facts.quote: The curved structural elements of the station building were constructed using technologies developed and previously deployed by the architecture firm. These were formed primarily of concrete, which had been supported and shaped by prefabricated steel units combined with temporary moulds created by CNC-milling, allowing for complex shapes, durability and strength.

facts.fact: Bolzano's museum of modern and contemporary art, founded in 1985.
facts.quote: The Museion (from the greek μουσείον, meaning the temple of the muses) is the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art of Bolzano, in South Tyrol, Italy. It was founded in 1985.

facts.fact: Its new building in central Bolzano, by KSV Krüger Schuberth Vandreike, opened on 24 May 2008.
facts.quote: On 24 May 2008 the Museion opened to the public its new venue, built by the KSV - Krüger Schuberth Vandreike architects in the center of Bolzano.

facts.fact: The building is a rectangular prism 54 m long, 25 m high and 23 m wide, with transparent front and rear facades.
facts.quote: The main building of the Museion is a rectangular prism measuring 54 metres long, 25 metres high and 23 metres wide, with transparent front and rear façades.

facts.fact: It is meant as a physical and symbolic link between two parts of the city.
facts.quote: The building is a physical and symbolic link between the two parts of the city of Bozen.

facts.fact: Its collection of 4,500 works is shown in themed rotations.
facts.quote: The Museion currently holds 4500 works of art, both from international and local artists, which are exhibited according to a theme-based rotation.

facts.fact: Its art library holds 25,000 volumes.
facts.quote: Specialised in modern and contemporary art, Museion's library holds 25,000 volumes, 50 subscriptions to art journals and 400 DVDs.

facts.fact: Two curved blocks of 68 housing association flats in Kensal Green, London, designed by Maxwell Fry and completed in 1937.
facts.quote: Kensal House is a housing estate of two curved blocks of 68 housing association flats at the northern end of Ladbroke Grove, Kensal Green, completed in 1937 and designed by the architect Maxwell Fry.

facts.fact: It was the first modernist block in the UK designed for working-class tenants, and was seen as a prototype for modern living.
facts.quote: It was the first modernist block in the UK designed to be occupied by the working class and on completion in 1937, was widely thought to be a prototype for modern living.

facts.fact: The Gas Light and Coke Company commissioned and paid for it, to house 380 people.
facts.quote: The building was commissioned and financed by the Gas Light and Coke Company (GLCC) to provide 68 "working-class flats", housing 380 people.

facts.fact: It included a community centre, laundry, canteen and nursery school, and ran entirely on gas and coke, with no electricity.
facts.quote: The project included a community centre, communal laundry, canteen and a nursery school. The development was unusual in that there was no electricity provided, rather gas fires, coke fires, gas cookers, gas water heaters, and gas-powered irons.

facts.fact: Fry worked with a committee of five architects and the social reformer Elizabeth Denby.
facts.quote: The project was designed by Maxwell Fry, but was developed by a committee of five architects and the social reformer Elizabeth Denby, who had worked with Fry at the Peckham Pioneer Health Centre.

facts.fact: Fry wanted an urban village, and with Denby aimed to give working people healthier, happier, safer lives.
facts.quote: Fry wanted to create what he called an urban village, and he and Denby wanted to offer working people "healthier, happier, safer, and more fulfilling lives".

facts.fact: Its water pipes are set in the concrete floors, which makes repairs hard.
facts.quote: The issue is difficult to fix because Fry design the building such that the water pipes were embedded in the concrete floor, making them hard to access, while listed building status makes alterations legally difficult.

facts.fact: It has been Grade II* listed since 1981, as has its day nursery.
facts.quote: As of 1981 it is Grade II* listed with Historic England, as is the associated Kensal House Day Nursery.

facts.fact: A London railway terminus in Camden, one of the UK's busiest stations and the southern end of the East Coast Main Line to Yorkshire, the North East and Scotland.
facts.quote: King's Cross railway station, also known as London King's Cross, is a passenger railway terminus in the London Borough of Camden, on the edge of Central London. It is one of the busiest stations in the United Kingdom and the southern terminus of the East Coast Main Line to Yorkshire and the Humber, North East England and Scotland.

facts.fact: Lewis Cubitt, brother of the builder Thomas Cubitt and the engineer Sir William Cubitt, made the station's detailed design.
facts.quote: The station's detailed design was by Lewis Cubitt, the brother of Thomas Cubitt (the architect of Bloomsbury, Belgravia and Osborne House), and Sir William Cubitt (who was chief engineer of the Crystal Palace built in 1851, and consulting engineer to the GNR and South Eastern Railway).

facts.fact: Two great arched train sheds end in a brick front that echoes the arches behind, with a 34 m clock tower as its main feature.
facts.quote: The design comprised two great arched train sheds, with a brick structure at the south end designed to reflect the arches behind. Its main feature was a 112-foot (34 m) high clock tower that held treble, tenor and bass bells, the last of these weighing 1 ton 9 cwt (1.47 tonnes).

facts.fact: The biggest station in England at the time, it opened on 14 October 1852.
facts.quote: The station, the biggest in England at that time, opened on 14 October 1852.

facts.fact: A £500 million restoration, approved in 2007, reglazed the original arched roof and replaced the 1972 front extension with an open plaza.
facts.quote: The £500 million restoration plan announced by Network Rail in 2005 was approved by Camden London Borough Council in 2007. It involved restoring and reglazing the original arched train shed roof and removing the 1972 extension at the front of the station and replacing it with an open-air plaza.

facts.fact: The semi-circular departures concourse by John McAslan, west of the station behind the Great Northern Hotel, opened in March 2012.
facts.quote: The new semi-circular departures concourse opened to the public in March 2012. Situated to the west of the station behind the Great Northern Hotel, it was designed by John McAslan and built by Taylor Woodrow Construction.

facts.fact: Its architect says the concourse roof is Europe's longest single-span station structure: a 54 m radius with over 2,000 triangular panels, half of them glass.
facts.quote: The architect claimed that the roof is the longest single-span station structure in Europe and the semi-circular structure has a radius of 59 yards (54 m) and more than 2,000 triangular roof panels, half of which are glass.

facts.fact: The concourse's white steel roof grid, engineered by Arup, has been likened to a reverse waterfall.
facts.quote: The steel structure of the roof, engineered by Arup, has been described as being "like some kind of reverse waterfall, a white steel grid that swoops up from the ground and cascades over your head".

facts.fact: An art gallery in Chichester with one of the world's best collections of 20th-century British art.
facts.quote: Pallant House Gallery is an art gallery in Chichester, West Sussex, England. It houses one of the best collections of 20th-century British art in the world.

facts.fact: The original Pallant House is a Grade I listed Queen Anne townhouse of 1712, built for the wine merchant Henry Peckham.
facts.quote: Pallant House is a Grade I listed Queen Anne townhouse built in 1712 for wine merchant Henry "Lisbon" Peckham and his wife Elizabeth.

facts.fact: The house was restored in 1979 and opened as a gallery in 1982.
facts.quote: The building had been used as council offices since 1919. The building was restored in 1979, and the gallery opened in 1982.

facts.fact: A new wing by Sir Colin Wilson and Long & Kentish opened in June 2006.
facts.quote: A new wing was opened in June 2006, designed by Sir Colin Wilson and Long & Kentish.

facts.fact: The openly modern wing joins the Queen Anne house and won the 2007 Gulbenkian Prize.
facts.quote: The unashamedly modern block, which stands next to and integrates with the original Queen Anne building, won the 2007 Gulbenkian Prize; in the words of the judges, the juxtaposition creates "a vibrant relationship between old and new ... continued in a series of inspired contemporary installations" which are housed within.

facts.fact: It is believed to be the first UK art gallery heated and cooled by a geothermal system, with water pumped through 69 pipes 35 m below ground to heat pumps, roughly halving its carbon emissions.
facts.quote: It is believed to be the first art gallery in the UK which is heated and cooled by a geothermal system, using water pumped through 69 pipes descending 35 metres under the building, connected to reversible heat pumps, which roughly halves its carbon emissions.

facts.fact: A courtyard garden at the rear is by Christopher Bradley-Hole.
facts.quote: To the rear is a new courtyard garden, designed by Christopher Bradley-Hole, a Chelsea Flower Show gold medallist.

facts.fact: In 2006 Colin St John Wilson also gave the gallery works by artists including Freud, Hamilton, Kitaj, Paolozzi and Blake.
facts.quote: In 2006, architect Sir Colin St John Wilson donated works by Michael Andrews, Peter Blake, David Bomberg, Patrick Caulfield, Lucian Freud, Richard Hamilton, R. B. Kitaj, Eduardo Paolozzi, Walter Sickert and Victor Willing.

facts.fact: An art gallery of the University of Manchester, in Whitworth Park, with over 60,000 items in its collections.
facts.quote: The Whitworth is an art gallery in Manchester, England, containing over 60,000 items in its collections. The gallery is located in Whitworth Park and is part of the University of Manchester.

facts.fact: The Grade II listed original was built in 1895–1900 in a free Jacobean style to designs by J. W. Beaumont.
facts.quote: The Grade II listed gallery was built between 1895 and 1900 in a free Jacobean style to the designs of J.W. Beaumont.

facts.fact: It is red brick with terracotta bands and dressings and green slate roofs.
facts.quote: The gallery consisting of two storeys and a basement is constructed of red brick with bands and dressings of matching terracotta and has green slate roofs.

facts.fact: The architects MUMA carried out the refurbishment.
facts.quote: The refurbishment works, undertaken by architects MUMA envisaged the gallery reopening to the public by summer 2014, but complications delayed the opening.

facts.fact: A glass, stainless steel and brick extension of two wings reaches into the park from the back, the wings joined by a glass promenade.
facts.quote: Developers have constructed a glass, stainless steel and brick extension consisting of two wings which extend into Whitworth Park from the back of the gallery building. The wings are connected by a glass promenade.

facts.fact: Opened on 14 February 2015, the extension doubled the public space and linked the building to the park.
facts.quote: The extension, which opened on 14 February 2015, doubled the gallery's public space. It provides more space for displaying the more than 60,000 items in the gallery's collections and links the building to Whitworth Park.

facts.fact: It won a RIBA National Award in 2015 and was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize.
facts.quote: The refurbishment and extension work resulted in the development winning a RIBA National Award in 2015 and subsequently being shortlisted for the RIBA Stirling Prize.

facts.fact: It drew over 440,000 visitors in its first year and won the Art Fund's Museum of the Year in 2015.
facts.quote: The gallery received more than 440,000 visitors in its first year and was awarded the Art Fund's Museum of the Year prize in 2015.

facts.fact: The London embassy was one of Arne Jacobsen's unfinished projects, completed after his death in 1971 by his former employees Hans Dissing and Otto Weitling, as Dissing+Weitling.
facts.quote: Hans Dissing and Otto Weitling were key employees at Arne Jacobsen's office and they founded Dissing+Weitling in 1971 upon his death to continue and complete his unfinished projects. These included a city hall in Mainz, Germany, which was also extended by Dissing+Weitling in 2008, a holiday resort on the north German island of Fehmarn, the Danish Embassy in London.

facts.fact: Jacobsen's works list dates the Royal Danish Embassy in London to 1976–77.
facts.quote: Royal Danish Embassy, London, UK (1976–77)

facts.fact: A large glasshouse at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, for palms and other tropical and subtropical plants, completed in 1848.
facts.quote: The Palm House is a large palm house in the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in London, that specialises in growing palms and other tropical and subtropical plants. It was completed in 1848.

facts.fact: An upper walkway takes visitors up into the branches of the larger plants.
facts.quote: Features include an upper walkway, taking the visitor into the branches of the larger plants.

facts.fact: It was the first greenhouse built on this scale and the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron.
facts.quote: The Palm House was the first greenhouse to be built on this scale. It was also the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron.

facts.fact: Kew's director Sir William Hooker asked Decimus Burton for sketches of a new Palm House in 1844.
facts.quote: Sir William J. Hooker was appointed Director of the Royal Botanic Garden at Kew in 1841. As part of his plan to improve its image, Sir William asked Decimus Burton to draw up preliminary sketches of a new Palm House for review in 1844.

facts.fact: The iron-maker Richard Turner, who had built the Belfast palm house, later built the one at Kew.
facts.quote: Designed by Charles Lanyon, the building was completed in 1840. It was constructed by the iron-maker Richard Turner, who would later build the Palm House at Kew.

facts.fact: Burton rejected Turner's Gothic first plans and preferred the Neoclassical style that shaped the final design.
facts.quote: Burton initially disagreed with Turner's original plans, which adopted the Gothic style he had used in his prior works. Burton preferred the Neoclassical style which informed the design of the Palm House.

facts.fact: It houses the world's oldest pot plant, an Encephalartos altensteinii moved there in 1848.
facts.quote: The Palm House is host to the oldest pot plant in the world (an Encephalartos altensteinii) which was moved to the Palm House in 1848.

facts.fact: Kew plans to close it in 2027 for a five-year, £50 million renovation to make it carbon neutral.
facts.quote: In 2025, Kew Gardens announced that the Palm House would close for a five-year renovation in 2027. The project was planned to cost £50 million and would entail converting the Palm House into a carbon neutral structure.

facts.fact: A Grade I listed former royal residence in Brighton, built in three stages from 1787 as a seaside retreat for George, Prince of Wales, later George IV.
facts.quote: The Royal Pavilion (also known as the Brighton Pavilion) and its surrounding gardens form a Grade I listed former royal residence in Brighton, England. Beginning in 1787, it was built in three stages as a seaside retreat for George, Prince of Wales, who became the Prince Regent in 1811, and King George IV in 1820.

facts.fact: Henry Holland, designer of Carlton House, made the first enlargement in 1787.
facts.quote: In 1787, the prince commissioned the designer of Carlton House, Henry Holland, to enlarge the existing building.

facts.fact: John Nash redesigned and greatly extended it between 1815 and 1822; what stands today is his work.
facts.quote: Between 1815 and 1822, the designer John Nash redesigned and greatly extended the pavilion, and it is his work that is still visible today.

facts.fact: Its Mughal-inspired look, with bulbous domes, chhatri-topped minarets and cusped arches, is Nash's.
facts.quote: The current appearance, with its Mughal inspired features such as bulbous domes, chhatri-topped minarets and cusped arches, is the work of the architect John Nash, who extended the building starting in 1815.

facts.fact: The tented roofs of the Music and Banqueting Rooms use laminated timber with iron connectors, letting them span the rooms without central columns.
facts.quote: Nash brought to Brighton structural innovations pioneered in his earlier work on the Rotunda at Carlton House, particularly in the construction of the Music and Banqueting Rooms' distinctive tented roofs. These employed laminated timber construction techniques developed by Nash and his assistant William Nixon for the Carlton House Rotunda in 1814—a pioneering system using specialised iron connectors that allowed the roofs to span large ceremonial spaces without central supporting columns.

facts.fact: The interiors, mainly by Frederick Crace and Robert Jones, drew on Chinese and Indian fashion.
facts.quote: The fanciful interior design, primarily by Frederick Crace and the little-known decorative painter Robert Jones, was heavily influenced by both Chinese and Indian fashion (with Mughal and Islamic architectural elements).

facts.fact: The town of Brighton bought it from the government for £53,000 in 1850.
facts.quote: The Brighton Improvement Commissioners and the Brighton Vestry successfully petitioned the government to sell the Pavilion to the town for £53,000 in 1850 under the Brighton Royal Pavilion Act 1850 (13 & 14 Vict. c. v).

facts.fact: In the First World War it became a military hospital for wounded Indian Army soldiers.
facts.quote: During the First World War, the Pavilion, along with other sites in Brighton, was transformed into a military hospital. From December 1914 to January 1916, sick and wounded soldiers from the Indian Army were treated in the former palace.

facts.fact: A 120 m stainless steel, pin-like monument on O'Connell Street, Dublin's main street, on the site of the former Nelson's Pillar.
facts.quote: The Spire of Dublin, alternatively titled the Millennium Spire or the Monument of Light (Irish: An Túr Solais), is a large, stainless steel, pin-like monument 120 metres (390 ft) in height, located on the site of the former Nelson's Pillar (and prior to that a statue of William Blakeney) on O'Connell Street, the main thoroughfare of Dublin, Ireland.

facts.fact: It was chosen from 205 entries in an international open competition held in 1998.
facts.quote: The Spire, or Spire of Light, was chosen from 205 submissions in an international open competition held in 1998 by a committee chaired by the Lord Mayor of Dublin, Joe Doyle.

facts.fact: Ian Ritchie designed it, seeking an elegant and dynamic simplicity bridging art and technology.
facts.quote: The spire was designed by Ian Ritchie of Ian Ritchie Architects, who sought an "elegant and dynamic simplicity bridging art and technology".

facts.fact: It is made of eight hollow stainless steel cone sections, tapering from 3 m across at the base to 15 cm at the top.
facts.quote: The Spire consists of eight hollow stainless steel cone sections, the longest being 20 m (66 ft), which were installed on 21 January 2003. It is an elongated cone of diameter 3 m (9.8 ft) at the base, narrowing to 15 cm (5.9 in) at the top.

facts.fact: Two tuned mass dampers by Arup, inside the fifth section, counter sway; the steel was shot-peened to change how it reflects light.
facts.quote: It features two tuned mass dampers inside the fifth section from the bottom, designed by engineers Arup, to counteract sway. The steel underwent shot peening to alter the quality of light reflected from it.

facts.fact: The pattern around its base draws on a rock core sample from the site and the DNA double helix.
facts.quote: The pattern around the base of the Spire is based on a core sample of rock formation taken from the ground where the spire stands and the DNA double helix.

facts.fact: At dusk the base is lit and the top 10 m glows through 11,884 holes lit by LEDs.
facts.quote: At dusk, the base of the monument is lit and the top 10 m (33 ft) is illuminated through 11,884 holes through which light-emitting diodes shine.

facts.fact: It was shortlisted for the 2004 RIBA National Award and Stirling Prize.
facts.quote: 2004 RIBA National Award & Stirling Prize shortlist

facts.fact: A 1950s council housing estate in the City of London, built on a site bombed in the Second World War.
facts.quote: The Golden Lane Estate is a 1950s council housing complex in the City of London. It was built on the northern edge of the City, on a site devastated by bombing during the Second World War.

facts.fact: The partnership Chamberlin, Powell and Bon was formed when Geoffry Powell won the design competition in February 1952.
facts.quote: The partnership of Chamberlin, Powell and Bon was formed when on 26 February 1952 Geoffry Powell was announced as competition winner.

facts.fact: Density was high at 200 people per acre, yet 60% of the site is open space, thanks to taller buildings than usual in 1951.
facts.quote: The population density, at 200 persons per acre, was high—but 60% of the site area is open space, a figure made possible by building taller structures than was common in 1951.

facts.fact: The first phase opened in 1957; the estate was then enlarged to the west with three more buildings, including Crescent House.
facts.quote: The first phase of the estate was officially opened in 1957, as stated on the commemorative stone on Bowater House. Before completion, the estate was enlarged to the west as more land was acquired, with three buildings added later: Cullum Welch House, Hatfield House and Crescent House.

facts.fact: The maisonette blocks are faced in red and blue panels, and the tower in yellow.
facts.quote: The maisonette blocks are faced with panels in primary colours (red and blue on maisonette blocks and yellow on the tower block).

facts.fact: At 16 storeys, the central tower Great Arthur House was briefly Britain's tallest residential building.
facts.quote: The visual anchor of the design is the tower block of one-bedroomed flats, Great Arthur House, which provides a vertical emphasis at the centre of the development and, at 16 storeys, was on its completion briefly the tallest residential building in Britain.

facts.fact: The estate shows the influence of Le Corbusier, which the architects openly acknowledged.
facts.quote: Both the earlier work and that at Crescent House are clearly influenced by the work of Le Corbusier, an influence the architects were happy to acknowledge.

facts.fact: It is listed Grade II, with Crescent House at Grade II*.
facts.quote: The estate is listed at Grade II, except for Crescent House, which is listed at Grade II* in view of its importance as an example of post-war residential architecture.

facts.fact: Richard MacCormac designed Southwark station for the Jubilee Line Extension; it won the Royal Fine Art Commission Trust/BSkyB Millennium Building of the Year Award in 2000.
facts.quote: MacCormac's commercial clients included: Southwark tube station for the Jubilee Line Extension (Royal Fine Art Commission Trust/BSkyB Millennium Building of the Year Award 2000); the Wellcome Foundation Wing/Dana Centre at the Science Museum, London (Celebrating Construction Achievement Regnl Award for Greater London 2000); the Cable and Wireless training centre in Coventry (Royal Fine Art Commission/Sunday Times Building of the Year Award 1994) and a Tesco supermarket in Ludlow.

facts.fact: It is among the works of MacCormac's practice, MJP Architects (MacCormac Jamieson Prichard).
facts.quote: MJP Architects worked in a variety of sectors from early social housing schemes in Milton Keynes and several education projects at Oxford and Cambridge universities, through to the training centre for Cable and Wireless in Coventry, the Wellcome Wing of the Science Museum, London, the Ruskin Library at the University of Lancaster, the Southwark tube station for the Jubilee Line Extension, and the Coventry Phoenix Initiative.

facts.fact: A major London terminus on Euston Road and the terminal for Eurostar trains to Belgium, France and the Netherlands.
facts.quote: St Pancras International ( ) is a major central London railway terminus on Euston Road in the London Borough of Camden. It is the terminus for Eurostar services between the United Kingdom and Belgium, France and the Netherlands.

facts.fact: William Henry Barlow designed the station; its single-span roof, 210 m long, 73 m wide and 30 m high, made it then the largest enclosed space in the world.
facts.quote: The station was designed by William Henry Barlow, with wrought iron pillars supporting a single-span roof. At 689 feet (210 m) long by 240 feet (73 m) wide, and 100 feet (30 m) high, it was then the largest enclosed space in the world.

facts.fact: The space under the raised tracks was used for Burton beer, so the undercroft's columns and girders were laid out like a beer warehouse, using the length of a beer barrel as its unit.
facts.quote: Instead, due to the value of the land in such a location the lower area was used for freight, in particular beer from Burton. As a result, the undercroft was built with columns and girders, maximising space, set out to the same plans as those used for beer warehouses, and with a basic unit of length that of a beer barrel.

facts.fact: The roof is a wrought-iron lattice frame, glazed over the middle half and covered with timber and slate on the outer quarters.
facts.quote: The single-span overall roof was the largest such structure in the world at the time of its completion. The materials used were wrought iron framework of lattice design, with glass covering the middle half and timber (inside)/slate (outside) covering the outer quarters.

facts.fact: After the station opened on 1 October 1868, George Gilbert Scott's ornate Gothic red-brick Midland Grand Hotel was built across its front.
facts.quote: Following the station's opening 1 October 1868, the MR built the Midland Grand Hotel on the station's façade. George Gilbert Scott won the competition to design it, with an ornate Gothic red-brick scheme.

facts.fact: In the 1960s plans to close it and demolish the hotel were defeated by a campaign led by John Betjeman.
facts.quote: By the 1960s, St Pancras was seen as redundant, and several attempts were made to close it and demolish the hotel (by then known as St Pancras Chambers). These attempts provoked strong and successful opposition, with the campaign led by the later Poet Laureate, John Betjeman.

facts.fact: It was listed Grade I in November 1967.
facts.quote: The station was given Grade I listed building status in November 1967, preventing any drastic modifications.

facts.fact: An £800 million refurbishment made it the terminal of High Speed 1; Queen Elizabeth II opened it in November 2007.
facts.quote: At the start of the 21st century, the complex underwent an £800 million refurbishment to become the terminal for the Channel Tunnel Rail Link, commonly known as High Speed 1, as part of an urban regeneration plan across East London, and opened by Queen Elizabeth II in November 2007.

facts.fact: A high-rise on the University of Strathclyde's John Anderson Campus in Glasgow, named after David Livingstone.
facts.quote: The Livingstone Tower is a prominent high rise building in Glasgow, Scotland and is a part of the University of Strathclyde's John Anderson Campus. The building was named after David Livingstone.

facts.fact: It was built in 1962–1964 as Alec House, a commercial office building.
facts.quote: The Livingstone Tower was constructed between 1962 and 1964 as Alec House – a commercial office building in a partnership between Glasgow Corporation, the former Royal College of Science and Technology and a commercial development company.

facts.fact: It is reinforced concrete, clad in a curtain wall of opaque dark green glass spandrel panels framed by orange metal uprights.
facts.quote: The building is of reinforced concrete construction and was state of the art in its construction methods at the time – being clad with a curtain wall in opaque dark green glass spandrel panels framed by orange metal uprights.

facts.fact: It had four Otis Autotronic high-speed lifts that responded to traffic in the building at different times of day.
facts.quote: With its original commercial use in mind, it featured an advanced elevator system for its day – four Otis Autotronic high speed lifts (also used in St. Andrew House on Sauchiehall Street) which were capable of responding to the traffic flow within the building at specific times of the day.

facts.fact: The tower stands on a three-storey concrete podium shared with the McCance Building, a car park and shops.
facts.quote: The tower sits atop a 3-storey concrete podium shared with the neighbouring McCance Building, an NCP car park, and a row of retail units at street level on George Street.

facts.fact: Set high on the Rottenrow drumlin, it is the campus's tallest structure and is seen across Glasgow's East End.
facts.quote: The building is the tallest structure on the John Anderson Campus, and is a notable landmark in the eastern side of the city centre, and its high position on the drumlin of Rottenrow means it can be seen from some considerable distance throughout the city's East End.

facts.fact: The tower is arguably International Style, unlike the Brutalist buildings attached to it.
facts.quote: The tower itself (arguably designed in the International Style) follows a contrasting architectural paradigm to the rest of the attaching buildings, which are of a distinctly Brutalist style – fashionable in the 1960s.

facts.fact: A 2010 refurbishment replaced the outer spandrel panels.
facts.quote: The building received a refurbishment in 2010, which saw internal realignment of some rooms and facilities, replacement of the outer spandrel panels, a new modern languages centre built, and the floors redesignated by transposing the ground floor to level 1, thus the former roof terrace becoming Level 15.

facts.fact: Billed as the world's first purpose-built modern centre for live storytelling, it stands on the High Street on Edinburgh's Royal Mile.
facts.quote: The Scottish Storytelling Centre, the world's first purpose-built modern centre for live storytelling, is located on the High Street in Edinburgh's Royal Mile, Scotland.

facts.fact: It opened on 1 June 2006.
facts.quote: It was formally opened on 1 June 2006 by Patricia Ferguson MSP, Minister for Culture in the Scottish Executive.

facts.fact: Malcolm Fraser Architects designed the building, which replaced the Netherbow Arts Centre and incorporates John Knox House.
facts.quote: The new building, designed by Malcolm Fraser Architects, replaced the former Netherbow Arts Centre, which itself replaced the Moray-Knox Church, demolished in the 1960s. It incorporates John Knox House.

facts.fact: It won a RIBA Award in 2007.
facts.quote: Scottish Storytelling Centre, Edinburgh: 2006 Winner, RIBA Award: 2007

facts.fact: In 2017 it was nominated for Best Performing Arts Venue in the Sunday Herald Culture Awards.
facts.quote: In 2017, the centre was nominated for Best Performing Arts Venue in the Sunday Herald Culture Awards.

facts.fact: Swansea Council's main administrative building, formerly County Hall, on the seafront overlooking Swansea Bay, about 800 m from the city centre.
facts.quote: Swansea Civic Centre (Welsh: Canolfan Ddinesig Abertawe) – formerly known as County Hall – is the principal administrative centre of Swansea Council. Standing some 800 m southwest of Swansea city centre, by the seafront and overlooking Swansea Bay, the complex houses – in addition to the council chamber and offices – a public cafe, the central library, an exhibition space, archives service, and contact centre.

facts.fact: It was built on the site of an old railway goods yard of the Mumbles Railway.
facts.quote: Finding that this arrangement, which involved sharing facilities with Swansea Council, to be inadequate, county leaders procured a dedicated building, selecting a site formerly occupied by an old railway goods yard associated with the Mumbles Railway.

facts.fact: C. W. Quick of the West Glamorgan County Architects Department designed it in the Brutalist style; it opened as County Hall in July 1982.
facts.quote: The new building was designed by C. W. Quick of the West Glamorgan County Architects Department in the Brutalist style, built by French Kier (phase 1) and A. Monk (phase 2) and opened as County Hall in July 1982.

facts.fact: The facades have continuous bands of glazing between deep washed calcined-flint panels.
facts.quote: The design featured continuous bands of glazing with deep washed calcined flint panels above and below.

facts.fact: Renamed Swansea Civic Centre in 2008, it also took in the city's central library.
facts.quote: It was renamed Swansea Civic Centre on 19 March 2008, and Swansea Central Library moved into the complex as part of a redevelopment scheme.

facts.fact: In 2016 the council announced plans that would demolish it for a city beach, aquarium and science centre.
facts.quote: In January 2016, Swansea Council announced plans to redevelop the area, the second phase of which would involve demolition of Swansea Civic Centre and the creation of city beach which would also include an aquarium and digital science centre.

facts.fact: In 2021 the Twentieth Century Society put it on its Top 10 Buildings at Risk list.
facts.quote: In May 2021 the Twentieth Century Society placed the site on its Top 10 Buildings at Risk List.

facts.fact: A cycle and foot bridge over the River Foyle in Derry, opened on 25 June 2011, linking Ebrington Square with the city centre.
