facts.quote: The Peace Bridge is a cycle and foot bridge across the River Foyle in Derry, Northern Ireland. It opened on 25 June 2011, connecting Ebrington Square with the rest of the city centre.

facts.fact: The 235 m bridge was designed by AECOM and Wilkinson Eyre Architects.
facts.quote: The 235 metres (771 ft) bridge was designed by AECOM, who also designed the Sutong Yangtze River Bridge, and Wilkinson Eyre Architects, who also designed the Gateshead Millennium Bridge.

facts.fact: It aims to improve relations by linking the largely unionist Waterside on the east bank with the largely nationalist Cityside on the west.
facts.quote: It is intended to improve relations between the largely unionist Waterside on the east bank with the largely nationalist Cityside on the west bank, by improving access between these areas, as part of wider regeneration plans.

facts.fact: The asymmetrical bridge, 4 m wide, hangs from two sloping pillars that symbolise the two communities coming together.
facts.quote: The asymmetrical bridge, which is 235 m (770 ft) long and 4 m (13 ft) metre wide, is supported by two sloping pillars and symbolises a coming-together of the two communities.

facts.fact: Its curved path links the Guildhall with Ebrington Square and St Columb's Park.
facts.quote: Its curved footpath, track and cycleway link the Guildhall, in the centre of the city, with Ebrington Square in the Waterside area, and St. Columb's Park.

facts.fact: It also crosses the railway line into Waterside station.
facts.quote: The bridge also provides a crossing over the railway line approaching Waterside station.

facts.fact: Its £14 million funding came from Northern Irish and Irish government departments, with matching money from the SEUPB Peace III programme.
facts.quote: The bridge was funded jointly by the Department for Social Development (NI), the Department of the Environment, Community and Local Government along with matching funding, totalling £14 million, from the SEUPB Peace III programme.

facts.fact: London Zoo bought the gorilla Mok in 1932, and Berthold Lubetkin designed a new gorilla house for him.
facts.quote: Mo Koundje ('Mok'), a western lowland gorilla, was purchased by the zoo in 1932. A new gorilla house was designed for him by Berthold Lubetkin.

facts.fact: The Gorilla House was one of the first projects of Lubetkin's London practice Tecton, alongside the Penguin Pool.
facts.quote: In London he set up the architectural practice Tecton. The first projects of Tecton included landmark buildings for London Zoo, the Gorilla House and a penguin pool (clearly showing the influence of Naum Gabo).

facts.fact: An art gallery in St Ives, Cornwall, showing modern British artists linked to the area.
facts.quote: Tate St Ives is an art gallery in St Ives, Cornwall, England, exhibiting work by modern British artists with links to the St Ives area.

facts.fact: It was built in 1988–1993 on the site of an old gasworks, overlooking Porthmeor Beach.
facts.quote: The Tate St Ives was built between 1988 and 1993 on the site of an old gasworks and looks over Porthmeor beach.

facts.fact: Tate commissioned Eldred Evans and David Shalev to design it in a style similar to the gasworks it replaced.
facts.quote: In 1988, the group purchased a former gasworks and commissioned architects Eldred Evans and David Shalev, to design a building for the gallery in a similar style to the gas works.

facts.fact: Building began in 1991; at its centre is a rotunda looking over Porthmeor Beach.
facts.quote: The building began in 1991, funded by the European Regional Development Fund, the Henry Moore Foundation and donations from the public. It included a rotunda at the centre of the gallery, looking over Porthmeor Beach and was completed in 1993.

facts.fact: Opened in June 1993, it was Tate's second regional gallery after Tate Liverpool.
facts.quote: The gallery opened in June 1993, the second of the Tate's regional galleries after Tate Liverpool, receiving more than 120,000 visitors before the end of the year.

facts.fact: A 1,200 m2 extension by Jamie Fobert was added, with the original architects involved in work on the existing building.
facts.quote: The building contract was awarded to BAM Construct UK, who would be adding a 1,200 square metres (13,000 sq ft) extension designed by Jamie Fobert, with the original architect's involvement in works to the existing building.

facts.fact: It won the Art Fund Museum of the Year Prize in July 2018.
facts.quote: In July 2018, Tate St. Ives won the Art Fund Museum of the Year Prize, beating the other shortlisted museums (the Brooklands Museum, the Ferens Art Gallery, Glasgow Women's Library and the Postal Museum, London) to the £100,000 prize.

facts.fact: The new building was shortlisted for the 2018 Stirling Prize.
facts.quote: Later that month, the Royal Institute of British Architects announced that the new Tate building had reached the shortlist for the 2018 Stirling Prize.

facts.fact: A 127 m observation tower on the south bank of the Clyde, part of Glasgow Science Centre; it holds the Guinness record as the tallest structure that can rotate fully, all 360 degrees.
facts.quote: Glasgow Tower (formerly known as the Millennium Tower) is a 127 metres (417 ft) free-standing landmark observation tower located on the south bank of the River Clyde in Glasgow, Scotland, and is part of the Glasgow Science Centre complex. It holds a Guinness World Record for being the tallest fully rotating freestanding structure in the world, in which the whole structure is capable of rotating 360 degrees.

facts.fact: Richard Horden designed it in 1992, first as a landmark for St Enoch Square; it was completed in 2001.
facts.quote: The Glasgow Tower is currently the tallest building in Glasgow and Scotland, and has held these records since its completion in 2001. It was designed by architect Richard Horden in 1992 and was initially proposed as a landmark for the city, with a proposal to build the tower in city's St Enoch Square.

facts.fact: Shaped like an aerofoil, a wing stood on end, it is turned into the wind by four 6 kW motors to cut wind resistance and keep it stable.
facts.quote: The tower is in the shape of an aerofoil (as if a symmetrical aircraft wing had been set in the ground vertically), with 4 manually operated 6 kW motors to turn it into the wind to reduce wind resistance and improve stability through aerodynamic forces (wind split by the aerofoil applies an equal force to both sides of the structure, holding it in place).

facts.fact: Buro Happold did the engineering; after commissioning, Glasgow architects BDP took over the project, which cost £10 million.
facts.quote: The original architectural design was by the architect Richard Horden, with engineering design by Buro Happold, but after commissioning the project was taken over by the Glasgow architects BDP. In the end, the tower cost £10 million.

facts.fact: The tower stands on a ring of 24 rubber-sprung roller bearings rather than being fixed to its foundations, so it can turn into the wind.
facts.quote: The tower itself is not directly connected to these foundations, instead being supported by a ring of 24 rubber-sprung roller bearings at Podium level. This is to allow the building to rotate to face into the wind.

facts.fact: The tower is clad in aluminium, while the Science Centre's other buildings use titanium and stainless steel.
facts.quote: Each of the three buildings is clad in a different metal. Titanium is used on the IMAX, stainless steel on the Science Mall and aluminium on Glasgow Tower.

facts.fact: It stands where the rotating Clydesdale Bank Tower stood for the 1988 Glasgow Garden Festival.
facts.quote: The structure occupies the same site where an earlier observation tower was built for the Glasgow Garden Festival in 1988 – that structure, known as the Clydesdale Bank Tower featured a rotating gondola that ascended up a central spine.

facts.fact: Problems with the thrust bearing it turns on closed it from February 2002 to August 2004.
facts.quote: Problems with the Nigerian-made thrust bearing on which it rotates led to it being closed between February 2002 and August 2004.

facts.fact: The Roman Catholic chaplaincy of the University of Edinburgh, begun in 1931 when the Dominicans moved into the house.
facts.quote: St Albert's Catholic Chaplaincy is the Roman Catholic chaplaincy for the University of Edinburgh. It started in 1931, when the Dominican Order moved into the house.

facts.fact: The original house is category A listed; the 2012 chapel won a RIBA award for architectural excellence.
facts.quote: The original building is category A listed and the chapel, built in 2012, won an award for architectural excellence from the Royal Institute of British Architects.

facts.fact: The house was designed in 1766 and built by 1779 as part of George Square.
facts.quote: The original building was designed in 1766. It was built between 1766 and 1779, as part of the construction of George Square.

facts.fact: The new chapel, built in the garden, opened in July 2012, the first new Dominican chapel in Scotland since the Reformation.
facts.quote: In July 2012, the new chapel, built in the garden, was completed and opened. It was the first new Dominican chapel in Scotland since the Reformation.

facts.fact: Stuart Allan of Simpson & Brown designed it; it seats 150, and the window behind the altar looks straight onto the garden.
facts.quote: It was designed by Stuart Allan, of the architectural firm Simpson & Brown. It has a capacity of 150 people and the window behind the altar has a clear view of the garden.

facts.fact: In 2013 the chapel was recognised by the Scottish Civic Trust, the RIAS and RIBA.
facts.quote: In 2013, the new chapel received architectural awards and recognition from the Scottish Civic Trust, the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland, and the Royal Institute of British Architects.

facts.fact: An airport terminal at Heathrow, opened in 2008; its main building is the largest free-standing structure in the UK.
facts.quote: Heathrow Terminal 5 is an airport terminal at Heathrow Airport, the main airport serving London. Opened in 2008, the main building in the complex is the largest free-standing structure in the United Kingdom.

facts.fact: The Richard Rogers Partnership led the design, with Pascall+Watson on production design and Arup and Mott MacDonald as structural engineers.
facts.quote: The building's leading architects were from the Richard Rogers Partnership and production design was completed by aviation architects Pascall+Watson. The engineers for the structure were Arup and Mott MacDonald.

facts.fact: It cost £4 billion and took almost 20 years from idea to opening, including Britain's longest public inquiry.
facts.quote: The building cost £4 billion and took almost 20 years from conception to completion, including the longest public inquiry in British history.

facts.fact: Rogers, chosen in 1989, compared the design to the Centre Pompidou for its flexible use of space.
facts.quote: Planning studies for the terminal began in February 1988 and Richard Rogers Partnership was selected to design the terminal in 1989. Richard Rogers compared his design to the Centre Pompidou, an earlier project that has similar flexibility in its use of space.

facts.fact: The main building is 396 m long, 176 m wide and 40 m tall.
facts.quote: The main terminal building is 396 metres (1,299 ft) long, 176 metres (577 ft) wide and 40 metres (130 ft) tall.

facts.fact: A single-span, undulating steel roof covers its four storeys, with glass facades tilted 6.5 degrees from vertical.
facts.quote: Its four storeys are covered by a single-span undulating steel frame roof, with glass façades angled at 6.5 degrees to the vertical. The area covered by the roof is the size of five football pitches, and each section weighs 2,200 tonnes.

facts.fact: Tall cranes would have broken into the airport's radar field, so the roof was built on the ground and jacked up on eight custom towers.
facts.quote: The roof could not have been lifted with conventional cranes because it would have vertically intersected with the airport's radar field. Therefore, the roof was assembled on the ground using smaller cranes, then lifted into place by eight custom-built towers, each fitted with two hydraulic jacks to pull the roof up.

facts.fact: Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 14 March 2008.
facts.quote: Queen Elizabeth II officially opened Terminal 5 in a ceremony on 14 March 2008.

facts.fact: A modernist house on Frognal Way, Hampstead, built in 1935–1936 by Maxwell Fry.
facts.quote: The Sun House on Frognal Way, Frognal, Hampstead, London, UK, is a modernist house built in 1935–1936 by Maxwell Fry. It is a Grade II* listed building.

facts.fact: It is Grade II* listed.
facts.quote: The Sun House on Frognal Way, Frognal, Hampstead, London, UK, is a modernist house built in 1935–1936 by Maxwell Fry. It is a Grade II* listed building.

facts.fact: It is counted among Fry's best-known buildings of the 1930s.
facts.quote: Among Fry's well-known buildings of the 1930s are the Sun House, Frognal Lane, Hampstead (1936), and Miramonte in New Malden, Kingston, Surrey (1937).

facts.fact: The business school of the University of Oxford.
facts.quote: Saïd Business School (Oxford Saïd or SBS) is the business school at the Social Sciences Division of the University of Oxford in Oxford, England.

facts.fact: It was founded in 1996 with a £28 million donation from the Syrian-born businessman Wafic Saïd.
facts.quote: Saïd Business School was founded in 1996 when Syrian-born businessman Wafic Saïd offered the University a donation of £28 million.

facts.fact: Its building, designed by Edward Jones and Sir Jeremy Dixon, stands on Park End Street opposite Oxford station, on the site of the old Rewley Road station.
facts.quote: A site for the new premises was found on Park End Street, opposite Oxford railway station, on land formerly occupied by Oxford Rewley Road railway station. The building was designed by Edward Jones and Sir Jeremy Dixon.

facts.fact: It opened on 5 November 2001, amid a student protest over the donor's links to an arms deal.
facts.quote: The opening on 5 November 2001 was accompanied by a demonstration by students concerned about the controversial nature of Wafic Saïd's donation. Saïd was linked with the UK's signing of the Al-Yamamah arms deal.

facts.fact: The Thatcher Business Education Centre was added on the same site in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012 the Thatcher Business Education Centre, financed by a donation from Saïd, was opened on the Park End Street site.

facts.fact: Nelson Mandela opened the lecture theatre named after him in 2002.
facts.quote: Nelson Mandela visited the Saïd Business School at the invitation of Saïd in 2002, to open the lecture theatre named in his honour.

facts.fact: Building began in 1937 on the New Bodleian, on Broad Street opposite the Clarendon Building, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott.
facts.quote: By the 1920s, the Library needed further expansion space, and in 1937 building work began on the New Bodleian building, opposite the Clarendon Building on the northeast corner of Broad Street. The New Bodleian was designed by architect Sir Giles Gilbert Scott.

facts.fact: Completed in 1940, it was an innovative ziggurat design with 60% of the bookstack underground.
facts.quote: Construction was completed in 1940. The building was of an innovative ziggurat design, with 60% of the bookstack below ground level.

facts.fact: A tunnel under Broad Street linked it to the Old Bodleian, with a walkway, a book conveyor and pneumatic tubes for book orders.
facts.quote: A tunnel under Broad Street connects the Old and New Bodleian buildings, and contains a pedestrian walkway, a mechanical book conveyor and a pneumatic Lamson tube system which was used for book orders until an electronic automated stack request system was introduced in 2002.

facts.fact: The New Bodleian closed on 29 July 2011 for rebuilding.
facts.quote: The New Bodleian closed on 29 July 2011 prior to rebuilding.

facts.fact: It was rebuilt behind its original facade, with better storage for rare and fragile material and better facilities for readers and visitors.
facts.quote: The New Bodleian building was rebuilt behind its original façade to provide improved storage facilities for rare and fragile material, as well as better facilities for readers and visitors.

facts.fact: WilkinsonEyre designed the new building; it reopened as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.
facts.quote: The new building concept was designed by WilkinsonEyre and the MEP design was undertaken by engineering consultancy Hurley Palmer Flatt. It reopened to readers as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.

facts.fact: It is one of the five buildings that make up the Bodleian Library.
facts.quote: The Bodleian Library occupies a group of five buildings near Broad Street: the 15th-century Duke Humfrey's Library, the 17th-century Schools Quadrangle, the 18th-century Clarendon Building and Radcliffe Camera, and the 20th- and 21st-century Weston Library.

facts.fact: The rebuilt library was nominated for the 2016 Stirling Prize.
facts.quote: The building was nominated for the 2016 Sterling Prize.

facts.fact: A court building in Manchester, completed in 2007, housing the county court, High Court district registry, family court and probate registry.
facts.quote: Manchester Civil Justice Centre is a governmental building in Manchester, England. Completed in 2007, it houses Manchester's county court and the Manchester District Registry of the High Court, the city's family proceedings court, the district probate registry, and the regional and area offices of the Court Service.

facts.fact: It was the first major court complex built in Britain since the Royal Courts of Justice of 1882, and is nicknamed the filing cabinet for its cantilevered floors.
facts.quote: The Civil Justice Centre was the first major court complex built in Britain since George Edmund Street's Royal Courts of Justice in London completed in 1882. Its distinctive architecture has been nicknamed the "filing cabinet" because of its cantilever floors at the end of the building.

facts.fact: The design draws on Expressionist architecture and the dynamic lines of Futurism.
facts.quote: The design takes inspiration from Expressionist architecture, as well as the artistic Futurist movement of the 1920s which promotes dynamic lines and a sense of fluid movement.

facts.fact: Australian architects Denton Corker Marshall, with engineers Mott MacDonald, won the competition in August 2002.
facts.quote: In August 2002, the design proposal from Australian architects Denton Corker Marshall, with engineers Mott MacDonald, was announced as the winner.

facts.fact: The building is 80 m tall with 17 storeys, its west side facing the River Irwell.
facts.quote: The western side of the 80 metres (260 ft), 17-storey building faces the River Irwell.

facts.fact: Cantilevered fingers project at each end, and the west facade carries a 60 × 60 m suspended glass wall, the largest in Europe.
facts.quote: The structure is notable for "fingers" at each end, cantilevered over the lower levels. On the western facade is a 60 m × 60 m (200 ft × 200 ft) suspended glass wall which totals 11,000 square metres (120,000 sq ft) - the largest in Europe.

facts.fact: Its long, slim plan allows natural cross-ventilation and daylight in most areas.
facts.quote: The elongated form of the building allowed for natural cross-flow ventilation from the prevailing west-to-east facade. The slender plan allows natural light to permeate most areas of the building without the need to resort to electric lighting.

facts.fact: It was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2008.
facts.quote: Manchester Civil Justice Centre was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in May 2008.

facts.fact: A Grade I listed building at Liverpool's Pier Head, one of the Three Graces on the waterfront with the Cunard and Port of Liverpool Buildings.
facts.quote: The Royal Liver Building is a Grade I listed building in Liverpool, England. It is located at the Pier Head and along with the neighbouring Cunard Building and Port of Liverpool Building is one of Liverpool's Three Graces, which line the city's waterfront.

facts.fact: Opened in 1911, it was built as the head office of Royal Liver Assurance.
facts.quote: Opened in 1911, the building was the purpose-built home of Royal Liver Assurance.

facts.fact: Its foundation stone was laid on 11 May 1908.
facts.quote: The foundation stone was laid on 11 May 1908.

facts.fact: Walter Aubrey Thomas designed it in the Edwardian Baroque style; it is an early reinforced-concrete building, a design some thought impossible to build.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Walter Aubrey Thomas in the Edwardian Baroque style and built by Edmund Nuttall Limited. The building is an early example of a building constructed using reinforced concrete, and given the building's radical design was considered by some to "be impossible to build".

facts.fact: L. G. Mouchel & Partners advised on the structure.
facts.quote: The structural engineering advisor was L. G. Mouchel & Partners.

facts.fact: It has ten storeys, two of them in the roof, and a 5.5 m copper Liver bird by Carl Bernard Bartels tops each clock tower.
facts.quote: It has ten storeys, including two in the roof. An 18 ft (5.5 m) copper Liver bird stands on each clock tower, designed by Carl Bernard Bartels.

facts.fact: A pair of clock towers crowns the building.
facts.quote: The building is crowned by a pair of clock towers. The clocks were made by Gent and Co. of Leicester.

facts.fact: Its 7.6 m clock faces are larger than Big Ben's and are the UK's largest electrically driven clocks.
facts.quote: The clock faces are 7.6 m (25 ft) in diameter, larger than those of London's famous landmark, the Great Westminster Clock, holding the distinction of being the largest electronically driven clocks in the UK.

facts.fact: Designed in 1859 by Philip Webb and William Morris as Morris's family home, it was finished in 1860.
facts.quote: Co-designed in 1859 by the architect Philip Webb and the designer William Morris, it was created to serve as a family home for Morris. Construction was completed in 1860.

facts.fact: It was Webb's first project as an independent architect and the only house Morris ever built.
facts.quote: Red House would be Webb's first project as an independent architect, while it remained the only house that Morris ever built.

facts.fact: Built with Morris's ideals of craftsmanship, it is an early example of the Arts and Crafts movement.
facts.quote: It was constructed using Morris' ethos of craftsmanship and artisan skills and is an early example of what came to be known as the Arts and Crafts movement.

facts.fact: It has an L-shaped plan, two storeys and a steep red-tiled roof.
facts.quote: Unique in its design, Red House was designed to an L-shaped plan, with two stories and a high-pitched roof made of red tile.

facts.fact: Windows were placed to suit the rooms rather than an outer symmetry, so many window types appear, from tall casements to bull's-eye windows.
facts.quote: Windows were positioned to suit the design of the rooms rather than to fit an external symmetry; thus a variety of different window types are present, including tall casements, hipped dormers, round-headed sash-windows, and bull's eye windows.

facts.fact: It has no applied ornament; its decorative features, like the arches over the windows, do structural work.
facts.quote: The house lacked any applied ornamentation, with its decorative features instead serving constructional purposes, such as the arches over the windows, and the louvre in the open roof over the staircase.

facts.fact: Morris designed house and garden together; the garden was split into four small squares by rose trellises.
facts.quote: The garden was similarly unique in its design, with Morris insisting on integration of the design of the house and garden; the latter was divided into four small square gardens by trellises on which roses grew.

facts.fact: It was listed Grade I in 1950.
facts.quote: In 1950 it was designated a Grade I listed building by English Heritage.

facts.fact: A not-for-profit science centre in Holyrood, Edinburgh, beside the Scottish Parliament at the foot of Salisbury Crags.
facts.quote: Dynamic Earth (originally known as Our Dynamic Earth) is a not-for-profit visitor attraction and science centre in Edinburgh, and is Scotland's largest interactive visitor attraction. It is located in Holyrood, beside the Scottish Parliament building and at the foot of Salisbury Crags.

facts.fact: It stands near where the geologist James Hutton lived and worked in the 18th century.
facts.quote: The project is located close to where Scottish geologist James Hutton lived and worked in the city in the 18th century.

facts.fact: The site was formerly a gasworks and part of the old Holyrood Brewery.
facts.quote: The location was previously on a site which was latterly a gas-works and part of the old Holyrood Brewery.

facts.fact: It cost about £34 million and was the first major UK millennium attraction to open.
facts.quote: The exhibition cost around £34 million to design and construct (out of a budget of £150 million for the entire area) and was the first major United Kingdom millennium attraction to open.

facts.fact: Michael Hopkins and Partners designed it: a membrane held up by steel masts, stretched over a steel skeleton.
facts.quote: The building's structure consists of a steel mast-supported membrane stretched over a steel skeleton. It was designed by architects Michael Hopkins and Partners.

facts.fact: The design keeps the old outer wall of the Abbey Brewery ale stores that stood on the site.
facts.quote: The design incorporates the original wall that formed the outer perimeter of the Abbey Brewery ale stores that were formerly on the site.

facts.fact: Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1999.
facts.quote: The centre was officially opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1999.

facts.fact: The building won a Civic Trust Award in 2000 and a RIBA Regional Award in 2001.
facts.quote: The building itself has also won a 2001 RIBA Regional Award from the Royal Institute of British Architects and a Civic Trust Award in 2000.

facts.fact: A former Church of Scotland parish church in Glasgow, and the only church by Charles Rennie Mackintosh ever built.
facts.quote: Queen's Cross Church is a former Church of Scotland parish church in Glasgow, Scotland. It is the only church designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh to have been built; hence, it is also known as The Mackintosh Church.

facts.fact: The Free Church of St Matthew commissioned it in 1896 from Honeyman and Keppie, where John Honeyman gave the job to the young Mackintosh.
facts.quote: In 1896, the Free Church of St Matthew, Glasgow, commissioned a new church and hall from the experienced Glasgow architectural practice of Honeyman and Keppie, to be located within the developing area of Springbank, near Maryhill. John Honeyman allocated the job to his young, talented, trainee architect, Charles Rennie Mackintosh.

facts.fact: The awkward corner site was hemmed in by tenements and a warehouse, and the Free Church wanted a simple design.
facts.quote: The site was an awkward one, being on a corner plot and butted by tenements and a large warehouse. In keeping with their beliefs, the Free Church required simplicity in design.

facts.fact: The memorial stone was laid in June 1898 and the first service held on 10 September 1899.
facts.quote: A memorial stone was laid on 23 June 1898 and the church held its first service on 10 September 1899.

facts.fact: It has no tall spire; its squat south-west tower was modelled on one at Merriott in Somerset.
facts.quote: Unlike many churches in Glasgow, Mackintosh's church doesn't have a huge towering spire, and is rather squat and more like a Norman Castle, called 'Modern gothic' by other architects. The main south-west tower was modelled on one at Merriot in Somerset which Mackintosh visited in 1895.

facts.fact: A timber-lined barrel-vaulted roof spans the full forty feet of the nave.
facts.quote: The roof is made up by a striking timber-lined barrel-vaulted roof, which spans the entire forty feet of the nave.

facts.fact: The pulpit is carved with a Mackintosh motif repeated five times around its curved front.
facts.quote: The pulpit is carved in Mackintosh designs, which repeat five times around the curved front. It has been suggested that it represents the wings of a bird protecting young shoots - sown on fertile ground.

facts.fact: Closed as a church in the 1970s, it is now home to the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society.
facts.quote: After the church was decommissioned in the 1970s, unlike many churches which were converted to theatres, apartments or demolished and because of the popularity of Mackintosh's work, the church became home of the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society, which owns and operates the church as a tourist attraction.

facts.fact: Built in 1897 to designs by William Frame, it replaced the Bute Dock Company's headquarters, which burned down in 1892.
facts.quote: The building was built in 1897 and designed by the English architect William Frame. It was a replacement for the headquarters of the Bute Dock Company which burnt down in 1892.

facts.fact: Frame's mentor was William Burges, with whom he worked on Cardiff Castle and Castell Coch.
facts.quote: Frame's mentor was William Burges, with whom he worked on the rebuilding of Cardiff Castle and Castell Coch until Burges's death in 1881.

facts.fact: A coat of arms on the facade carries the company motto 'by water and fire', the elements of steam power.
facts.quote: A coat of arms on the building's façade bears the company's motto "Wrth ddŵr a thân" ("by water and fire"), encapsulating the elements creating the steam power which transformed Wales.

facts.fact: In a French-Gothic Renaissance style, it has hexagonal chimneys, carved friezes, gargoyles and a highly ornamental clock tower.
facts.quote: Incorporating a French-Gothic Renaissance theme, the Pierhead boasts details such as hexagonal chimneys, carved friezes, gargoyles, and a highly ornamental and distinctive clock tower.

facts.fact: The exterior is glazed terracotta blocks from J. C. Edwards & Co. of Acrefair, near Ruabon.
facts.quote: Its exterior is finished in glazed terracotta blocks supplied at the end of the 19th century by J. C. Edwards & Co. of Acrefair, near Ruabon in Wrexham County Borough; they were once described as one of the most successful producers of terracotta in the world.

facts.fact: Its architecture and role in the growth of the docks and industrial Wales earned it Grade I listing.
facts.quote: These features, along with the Pierhead's role in the development of the docks, Cardiff and industrial Wales, earned it the status of a Grade I listed building.

facts.fact: It became the Port of Cardiff's administrative office in 1947.
facts.quote: The building became the administrative office for the Port of Cardiff in 1947.

facts.fact: It is now part of the Senedd estate, and its clock is nicknamed the Big Ben of Wales.
facts.quote: The Pierhead Building is part of the estate of the Senedd (Welsh Parliament; Welsh: Senedd Cymru), which also includes the Senedd building and Tŷ Hywel. The clock on the building is unofficially known as the "Baby Big Ben" or the "Big Ben of Wales".

facts.fact: The museum, first called the Belfast Municipal Museum and Art Gallery, moved to its present site in Stranmillis in 1929.
facts.quote: Originally called the Belfast Municipal Museum and Art Gallery, in 1929, it moved to its present location in Stranmillis.

facts.fact: The 1929 building was designed by James Cumming Wynne.
facts.quote: The new building was designed by James Cumming Wynne.

facts.fact: A major extension by Francis Pym, who won the 1964 competition, opened in 1972 and was Pym's only completed work.
facts.quote: A major extension constructed by McLaughlin & Harvey Ltd to designs by Francis Pym who won the 1964 competition was opened in 1972 and Pym's only completed work.

facts.fact: Until it was altered, the extension was the most important example of Brutalism in Northern Ireland.
facts.quote: It was published in several magazines and was until alteration the most important example of Brutalism in Northern Ireland.

facts.fact: David Evans praised the power of its great cubic projections and cantilevers above the conifers of the Botanic Gardens.
facts.quote: It was praised by David Evans for the "almost barbaric power of its great cubic projections and cantilevers brooding over the conifers of the botanic gardens like a mastodon".

facts.fact: The later redevelopment was criticised, including by the Twentieth Century Society, for changing the Brutalist character and dismantling the spiral sequence of rooms in Pym's extension.
facts.quote: The redevelopment drew criticism from many significant figures in the architectural community and the Twentieth Century Society, especially for changes to the Brutalist character and dismantling of the spiral sequence of rooms in the Pym extension.

facts.fact: The museum reopened in October 2009, eighty years to the day after its original opening.
facts.quote: The museum reopened in October 2009, eighty years to the day since its original opening.

facts.fact: The Basilica of Our Lady, Queen of Ireland is a Roman Catholic basilica in Knock, County Mayo, Ireland.
facts.quote: The Basilica of Our Lady, Queen of Ireland is a Roman Catholic basilica church of the Latin Church located in the small town of Knock, in County Mayo in Ireland.

facts.fact: It was designed in a modern style in concrete by Daithi Hanly with Louis J Brennan and Brian Brennan, and completed in 1976.
facts.quote: It was designed in modern architecture style with concrete materials by architect Daithi Hanly, and by architects Louis J Brennan and Brian Brennan, and completed in 1976.

facts.fact: Its construction was overseen by Monsignor James Horan, parish priest of Knock.
facts.quote: Its construction was overseen by Monsignor James Horan, who was the parish priest of Knock from 1967 until his death in 1986.

facts.fact: Pope John Paul II raised the shrine to the status of Minor Basilica on 17 July 1979.
facts.quote: Pope John Paul II raised the shrine to the status of Minor Basilica via his decree Abunde Constat Quam on 17 July 1979.

facts.fact: The basilica holds about 10,000 people and is part of the Knock Shrine grounds, with four other churches.
facts.quote: The basilica, which can accommodate approximately 10,000 people, serves the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Tuam, and it is part of the Knock Shrine grounds that incorporates four other churches, including the Apparition Church, the place where, according to Catholic beliefs, on Thursday evening of 21 August 1879, the Blessed Virgin Mary, Saint Joseph, and Saint John the Evangelist are proposed to have appeared, the old parish church, the Blessed Sacrament Chapel, and the Chapel of Reconciliation.

facts.fact: Lys Kernow, called New County Hall from 1966 to 2009, is a municipal building on Treyew Road in Truro, Cornwall.
facts.quote: Lys Kernow ([lɪːz ˈkɛrnɔʊ]; English: Court of Cornwall), known as New County Hall between 1966 and 2009, is a municipal facility at Treyew Road in Truro, Cornwall.

facts.fact: It is the headquarters of Cornwall Council and a Grade II listed building.
facts.quote: The building, which serves as the headquarters of Cornwall Council, is a Grade II listed building. == History == During the first half of the 20th century Cornwall County Council held its meetings at the Old County Hall at Station Road in Truro.

facts.fact: It was designed in the Brutalist style by the Duchy Architect Francis Kenneth Hicklin and his successor Alan Groves, and opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 14 July 1966.
facts.quote: The new building was designed by the Duchy Architect, Francis Kenneth Hicklin, and his successor, Alan Groves, in the Brutalist style and was officially opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 14 July 1966.

facts.fact: It is a three-storey square concrete-framed building with about 50 bays on each side, each bay a window per floor between concrete slabs.
facts.quote: The design involved a three-storey square concrete-framed structure with circa 50 bays on each side; the bays contained a window on each floor flanked by concrete slabs.

facts.fact: The council chamber, on the first floor, is cantilevered out of the main building on the east side.
facts.quote: Internally, the principal room was the council chamber which was on the first floor and was cantilevered out of the main building on the east side.

facts.fact: A central courtyard was landscaped by Sir Geoffrey Jellicoe, with a Barbara Hepworth sculpture unveiled there at the opening.
facts.quote: There was a courtyard, landscaped by Sir Geoffrey Jellicoe, in the centre of the building; a sculpture by Barbara Hepworth, known as "Rock form, Porthcurno", was unveiled in the courtyard garden when the building opened.

facts.fact: A refurbishment designed by Poynton Bradbury Wynter Cole of St Ives was completed in 2013.
facts.quote: This was followed by an extensive programme of refurbishment works, to a design by Poynton Bradbury Wynter Cole of St Ives, which was completed in 2013.

facts.fact: The house joins the medieval great hall of a former royal residence to an Art Deco extension added in the 1930s.
facts.quote: The house consists of the medieval great hall of a former royal residence, to which an Art Deco extension was added in the 1930s.

facts.fact: The great hall's hammerbeam roof is the third-largest of its type in England, and the Art Deco interior has been called a masterpiece of modern design.
facts.quote: The hammerbeam roof of the great hall is the third-largest of its type in England, and the Art Deco interior of the house has been described as a "masterpiece of modern design".

facts.fact: In 1933 Stephen and Virginia Courtauld leased the site and commissioned Seely & Paget to restore the hall and build a modern home attached to it.
facts.quote: In 1933, Stephen Courtauld and his wife Virginia "Ginie" Courtauld (née Peirano) acquired a 99-year lease on the palace site and commissioned Seely & Paget to restore the hall and create a modern home attached to it.

facts.fact: Seely and Paget added a minstrels' gallery and timber screen to the hall and based the main house on Christopher Wren's work at Hampton Court and Trinity College, Cambridge.
facts.quote: Seely and Paget added a minstrel's gallery and a timber screen to the hall, while creating a design for the main house inspired by Christopher Wren's work at Hampton Court Palace and Trinity College, Cambridge.

facts.fact: The interior was decorated in the Art Deco style.
facts.quote: The home was decorated internally in the Art Deco style.

facts.fact: The entrance hall, by Swedish designer Rolf Engströmer, is lit from a glazed dome that shows off its blackbean veneer and figurative marquetry.
facts.quote: The entrance hall was created by Swedish designer Rolf Engströmer; light floods in from a glazed dome, highlighting blackbean veneer and figurative marquetry.

facts.fact: The dining room, drawing room and Virginia Courtauld's circular bedroom and bathroom were designed by the Italian Piero Malacrida de Saint-August.
facts.quote: Other rooms in the house, including the dining room, drawing room and Virginia Courtauld's circular bedroom and adjoining bathroom, were the work of the Italian designer Piero Malacrida de Saint-August, while Seely and Paget designed many of the bedrooms.

facts.fact: English Heritage took over the palace in 1995 and finished major restorations of the interiors and gardens in 1999.
facts.quote: In 1995, English Heritage assumed management of the palace, and in 1999, completed major repairs and restorations of the interiors and gardens.

facts.fact: Hornsey Town Hall is a public building in Crouch End, Hornsey, London.
facts.quote: Hornsey Town Hall is a public building in Hatherley Gardens in the Crouch End area of Hornsey, London.

facts.fact: It is a Grade II* listed building.
facts.quote: It is a Grade II* listed building.

facts.fact: It was the first major UK building constructed in the Modernist style.
facts.quote: Hornsey Town Hall was the first major UK building to be constructed in the Modernist style.

facts.fact: New Zealand-born architect Reginald Uren designed it under the influence of Hilversum Town Hall, and the design won a RIBA bronze medal.
facts.quote: Designed by New Zealand-born architect Reginald Uren for the Municipal Borough of Hornsey, the building shows the influence of Hilversum Town Hall in the Netherlands and the design was awarded a bronze medal by the Royal Institute of British Architects.

facts.fact: It was opened by the Duke and Duchess of Kent on 4 November 1935.
facts.quote: It was built by Gee, Walker & Slater Ltd and opened by the Duke and Duchess of Kent on 4 November 1935.

facts.fact: A symmetrical seven-bay front faces a small courtyard, with wide steps to three canopied doorways and tall first-floor windows behind a wrought-iron balcony.
facts.quote: The design involved a symmetrical main frontage with seven bays facing onto a small courtyard in Hatherley Gardens with a wing of six bays enclosing the courtyard to the right; the main frontage featured wide steps leading up to three doorways with a canopy above on the ground floor; there were seven tall windows on the first floor with a wrought-iron balcony in front of the central three windows.

facts.fact: A tall tower with a flagpole stands at the corner of the courtyard.
facts.quote: A tall tower with a flag pole was erected at the corner of the courtyard.

facts.fact: In 1981 it became one of the first 1930s buildings to be listed.
facts.quote: In 1981, it became one of the first of the buildings constructed in the 1930s to achieve listed building status.

facts.fact: A restoration designed by Donald Insall Associates repaired the council chamber seating, signage, metal balustrades and parquet and terrazzo floors.
facts.quote: The restoration work, which was carried out to a design by Donald Insall Associates, involved reupholstered leather seating in the council chamber and repairs to the signage, metal balustrading, parquet flooring and terrazzo flooring.

facts.fact: The Shell Centre in London is the global headquarters of Shell plc.
facts.quote: The Shell Centre in London is the global headquarters of oil major Shell plc.

facts.fact: It stands on the South Bank of the Thames near County Hall, behind the London Eye.
facts.quote: It is a prominent feature on the South Bank of the River Thames near County Hall, and now forms the backdrop to the London Eye.

facts.fact: It was built between 1957 and 1962 to a design by Sir Howard Robertson; the tower is 107 metres tall with 27 storeys and three below ground.
facts.quote: The Shell Centre was constructed by Sir Robert McAlpine between 1957 and 1962, to a design by Sir Howard Robertson, and the tower stands at 107 metres (351 ft) with 27 storeys (26 numbered and a mezzanine level) and extends three storeys below ground.

facts.fact: It was the first London office tower taller than the Victoria Tower of the Palace of Westminster.
facts.quote: The tower was the first London office tower to exceed the height of the Victoria Tower of the Palace of Westminster.

facts.fact: Modern Movement critics denounced its Portland stone cladding and bronze-framed upright windows, and the buildings have generally been thought dull.
facts.quote: The choice of Portland Stone cladding, and bronze framed individual upright windows were denounced by Modern Movement critics, and the centre's buildings have generally been regarded as dull.

facts.fact: The traditional cladding has weathered better than most concrete or curtain-wall facades of the time.
facts.quote: However, the extremely traditional cladding has meant that the buildings have weathered better than most of their contemporaries with concrete or aggregate faced façades or curtain wall glazing.

facts.fact: The original interiors were luxurious and included work by Ernesto Nathan Rogers, who had worked on the Torre Velasca in Milan.
facts.quote: The original interiors were luxuriously appointed, and as well as contributions from a British design team (many of whom had worked on the Festival of Britain), they included work by Ernesto Nathan Rogers who had worked on the Torre Velasca in Milan.

facts.fact: Its air conditioning draws water from the Thames through a tunnel and returns it to the river.
facts.quote: Visible in the Thames at low tide just in line with the tower as water turbulence at one point a few feet into the river bed is the outflow point of the Shell Centre's air conditioning system, which sucks in river water from just outside County Hall and sends it via a pipe within a bolt iron tunnel (built exactly like a tube railway tunnel), to a point convergent with the outfall, beyond which both the intake pipe and the outflow pipes continue under the embankment and Jubilee Gardens to the basement of the tower.

facts.fact: The nine-storey wings of the Upstream Building have been replaced by new glazed towers around the original Shell tower.
facts.quote: The 9-storey ranges of the Upstream Building have now been replaced by a cluster of new predominantly glazed towers around the original Shell tower.

facts.fact: Newcastle Civic Centre is a municipal building in the Haymarket area of Newcastle upon Tyne, England.
facts.quote: Newcastle Civic Centre is a municipal building in the Haymarket area of Newcastle upon Tyne, England.

facts.fact: Designed by George Kenyon, it was built for Newcastle City Council in 1967 and opened by King Olav V of Norway on 14 November 1968.
facts.quote: Designed by George Kenyon, the centre was built for Newcastle City Council in 1967 and formally opened by King Olav V of Norway on 14 November 1968.

facts.fact: It is Grade II* listed and stands 200 feet (61 m) tall.
facts.quote: It is a Grade II* listed building and is the joint eighth-tallest building in the city, standing at 200 feet (61 m).

facts.fact: It was commissioned to replace a Victorian town hall in St Nicholas Square.
facts.quote: The civic centre was commissioned to replace a Victorian Town Hall which stood in St Nicholas Square (between the Bigg Market and the Cloth Market).

facts.fact: Construction by Sir Robert McAlpine began in May 1960.
facts.quote: The construction work, which was undertaken by Sir Robert McAlpine, commenced on the building in May 1960, and the foundation stone was laid by the Lord Mayor, Alderman Mrs Gladys Robson, on 30 November 1960.

facts.fact: It is known for its modern sculptures: David Wynne's River God Tyne and Swans in Flight, and John Robert Murray McCheyne's seahorses on top of the tower.
facts.quote: The Civic Centre is also notable for its modern sculptures, in particular the River God Tyne and Swans in Flight, both by David Wynne and the seahorses on the top of the tower by John Robert Murray McCheyne.

facts.fact: The former rates hall has two abstract murals by Victor Pasmore.
facts.quote: The cashiers reception of the former rates hall, now the Customer Service Centre, has two abstract murals by Victor Pasmore.

facts.fact: The Palace of Westminster in London is the meeting place of the Parliament of the United Kingdom.
facts.quote: The Palace of Westminster is the meeting place of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and is located in London, England.

facts.fact: It has been Grade I listed since 1970 and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
facts.quote: The palace has been a Grade I listed building since 1970 and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

facts.fact: A fire in 1834 destroyed most of the old palace, but the eleventh-century Westminster Hall survived and was built into the new one.
facts.quote: In 1834 a second, larger fire destroyed the majority of the palace, but the eleventh century Westminster Hall was saved and incorporated into the replacement building.

facts.fact: Charles Barry won the competition to design the new palace and chose a Gothic Revival style.
facts.quote: The competition to design the new palace was won by the architect Charles Barry, who chose a Gothic Revival style for the building.

facts.fact: Barry had little experience of Gothic and relied heavily on Augustus Pugin to design the details.
facts.quote: Barry was inexperienced with Gothic and relied heavily on Augustus Pugin to design details.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1840 and lasted 30 years, with delays, cost overruns and the deaths of Barry and Pugin.
facts.quote: Construction started in 1840 and lasted for 30 years, suffering delays, cost overruns, and the deaths of Barry and his assistant, Augustus Pugin.

facts.fact: The palace is known for its ornate decoration and helped spread Gothic Revival architecture elsewhere.
facts.quote: This new palace is notable for its ornate decoration, and contributed to the proliferation of Gothic Revival architecture in other places.

facts.fact: Its Elizabeth Tower houses the bell known as Big Ben.
facts.quote: The Elizabeth Tower of the palace houses the bell nicknamed Big Ben and is a landmark of London and the United Kingdom in general.

facts.fact: The Royal Crescent is a row of 30 terraced houses set out in a sweeping crescent in Bath, England.
facts.quote: The Royal Crescent is a row of 30 terraced houses laid out in a sweeping crescent in the city of Bath, England.

facts.fact: John Wood the Younger designed it, it was built between 1767 and 1774, and it is a Grade I listed example of Georgian architecture.
facts.quote: Designed by the architect John Wood, the Younger, and built between 1767 and 1774, it is among the greatest examples of Georgian architecture to be found in the United Kingdom and is a Grade I listed building.

facts.fact: The 500-foot (150 m) crescent has 114 Ionic columns on the first floor with a Palladian entablature above.
facts.quote: The 500-foot-long (150 m) crescent has 114 Ionic columns on the first floor with an entablature in a Palladian style above.

facts.fact: It was the first crescent of terraced houses ever built, an example of 'rus in urbe' with views over parkland.
facts.quote: It was the first crescent of terraced houses to be built and an example of "rus in urbe" (the country in the city) with its views over the parkland opposite.

facts.fact: Each buyer bought a length of the facade and hired their own architect to build a house behind it.
facts.quote: Each original purchaser bought a length of the façade, and then employed their own architect to build a house behind the facade to their own specifications; hence what can appear to be two houses is occasionally just one.

facts.fact: So the front is uniform and symmetrical, while the rear mixes different roof heights and windows.
facts.quote: This system of town planning is betrayed at the rear and can be seen from the road behind the Crescent: while the front is uniform and symmetrical, the rear is a mixture of differing roof heights, juxtapositions and fenestration.

facts.fact: A ha-ha in front makes an invisible boundary between the lower and upper lawns.
facts.quote: In front of the Royal Crescent is a ha-ha, a ditch on which the inner side is vertical and faced with stone, with the outer face sloped and turfed, making an effective but invisible partition between the lower and upper lawns.

facts.fact: In 1921 Robert Tor Russell took the Crescent as inspiration for Connaught Place in New Delhi.
facts.quote: In 1921, architect Robert Tor Russell used the Crescent as a source of inspiration to design the central business district of Connaught Place, New Delhi, India.

facts.fact: London Stadium is a multi-purpose outdoor stadium in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, London.
facts.quote: London Stadium (formerly and also known as the Olympic Stadium and the Stadium at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park) is a multi-purpose outdoor stadium at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in the Stratford district of London.

facts.fact: It was built for the 2012 Summer Olympics and Paralympics as the athletics venue and for their opening and closing ceremonies.
facts.quote: The stadium was originally constructed for the 2012 Summer Olympics and 2012 Summer Paralympics, serving as the athletics venue and as the site of their opening and closing ceremonies.

facts.fact: In 2006 LOCOG chose Sir Robert McAlpine and Populous to negotiate the design-and-build contract.
facts.quote: On 13 October 2006, the London Organising Committee of the Olympic and Paralympic Games (LOCOG) selected Sir Robert McAlpine and Populous to start exclusive negotiations to fulfil the design-and-build contract of the Stadium, after no other organisations met the bidding criteria.

facts.fact: The arena is dug into the site's soft clay, ringed by 25,000 permanent seats built on concrete rakers.
facts.quote: The stadium's track-and-field arena is excavated out of the soft clay found on the site, around which is permanent seating for 25,000, built using concrete "rakers".

facts.fact: A lightweight, demountable upper tier of steel and precast concrete held a further 55,000 spectators.
facts.quote: A lightweight demountable steel and pre-cast concrete upper tier was built up from this "bowl" to accommodate a further 55,000 spectators.

facts.fact: It used about 10,700 tons of steel, just under a quarter of the steel in Beijing's 2008 Olympic Stadium.
facts.quote: The stadium contains just under a quarter of the amount of steel used in the Olympic Stadium in Beijing for the 2008 Summer Olympics: about 10,700 tons.

facts.fact: Its compression truss reused surplus large-diameter North Sea gas pipes, and it also used recycled granite.
facts.quote: In addition to the minimal use of steel, which makes it 75 per cent lighter, the stadium also uses high-yield large diameter pipes that were surplus on completion of North Sea gas pipeline projects in its compression truss, and recycled granite.

facts.fact: The cable-supported roof covered about two-thirds of the seating.
facts.quote: The cable-supported roof structure covered approximately two-thirds of the stadium's seating.

facts.fact: It was shortlisted for the 2012 Stirling Prize, which went to the Sainsbury Laboratory in Cambridge.
facts.quote: The Olympic Stadium was nominated for the 2012 Stirling Prize in architecture losing out to the Sainsbury Laboratory at the University of Cambridge.

facts.fact: It held 80,000 for the Games and was remodelled between 2013 and 2015 with 66,000 seats.

facts.fact: With the structural engineer August Komendant, Kahn designed it as a concrete structure rather than a steel frame.
facts.quote: Kahn, relying on the expertise of August Komendant, a structural engineer and Kahn's preferred collaborator, instead designed the building as a concrete structure.

facts.quote: The Olivetti-Underwood Factory consists of 72 prestressed concrete units locked together in an 8x9 grid.

facts.fact: Each unit is a concrete shell 6 inches thick, 30 feet above the floor and 60 feet across, covering 3,600 square feet of roof.

facts.fact: The units' clipped corners leave a gap where four meet, letting daylight in through a translucent skylight.

facts.fact: The young Renzo Piano worked with Kahn for several months on the design, mainly on the roofing system.
facts.quote: Renzo Piano, a young Italian architect with an established practice in Genoa, used his connections with the Olivetti company to gain the equivalent of an internship with Kahn for several months while the factory was being designed, working primarily on the roofing system.

facts.fact: The Reynolds Metals Company International Headquarters is an International Style complex in a designed landscape near Richmond, Virginia, completed in 1958.
facts.quote: The Reynolds Metals Company International Headquarters is an International Style building complex set in a composed landscape in Henrico County, near Richmond, Virginia, completed in 1958.

facts.fact: Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed the low-rise Executive Office Building, with landscape architect Charles F. Gillette.
facts.quote: The low-rise Executive Office Building was designed by Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, in collaboration with Richmond landscape architect Charles F. Gillette.

facts.fact: The complex has been cited as a prototype for modern suburban office development.
facts.quote: The headquarters complex has been cited as a prototype for modern suburban office development.

facts.fact: It was meant to showcase the company's aluminium, used wherever possible, from the cladding to carpets and curtains.
facts.quote: Intended as a showcase for the products of the Reynolds Metals Company, the Executive Office Building incorporated aluminum, the company's principal product, wherever possible, principally in the building's exterior cladding, but even in interior furnishings and finishes, where carpets and draperies incorporated aluminum fibers.

facts.fact: The three-storey building rests on a raised podium.
facts.quote: The three-story building rests on an elevated podium.

facts.fact: An interior courtyard lights the inner spaces.
facts.quote: An interior courtyard illuminates interior spaces.

facts.fact: Deep fixed overhangs shade the south windows, and bright blue adjustable aluminium louvres control sun on the east and west.
facts.quote: Deep fixed overhangs on the south shade the windows from the sun, and are matched by non-functional overhangs on the north side. The east and west elevations feature bright blue adjustable aluminum louvers for sun control.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2000.

facts.fact: The Richard H. Mandel House is a historic home in Bedford Hills, Westchester County, New York.
facts.quote: The Richard H. Mandel House is a historic home located at Bedford Hills, Westchester County, New York.

facts.fact: Edward Durell Stone designed it, and it was built between 1933 and 1935 in the International Style.
facts.quote: It was designed by architect Edward Durell Stone and built between 1933 and 1935 in the International style.

facts.fact: The Z-shaped house overlooks the Croton Reservoir.
