facts.fact: It is a two-storey building of concrete block, steel frame and stucco, set into the sloping site.
facts.quote: It is a two-story, concrete block, steel frame, and stucco building with a partial basement recessed into the sloping site.

facts.fact: It has a flat roof, smooth walls without ornament, an asymmetrical horizontal composition, projecting balconies and wide ribbon windows.
facts.quote: It features a flat roof, smooth and uniform wall surfaces, lack of applied ornament, asymmetrical composition with an emphasis on horizontality, and projecting balconies and wide expanses of ribbon windows.

facts.fact: Donald Deskey designed the interiors and furnishings.
facts.quote: The interiors and furnishings for the home were designed by Donald Deskey.

facts.fact: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1996.
facts.quote: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1996.

facts.fact: River City is a mixed-use building at 800 South Wells Street in Chicago's South Loop.
facts.quote: River City is a mixed-use building at 800 South Wells Street in the South Loop neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois.

facts.fact: Bertrand Goldberg designed it, completed in 1986, sharing elements with his Marina City.
facts.quote: Completed in 1986, it was designed by Bertrand Goldberg and shares elements with his design for Marina City.

facts.fact: Beside the Chicago River, it has two serpentine 7- to 14-storey residential towers of poured-in-place concrete shells, with 449 homes.
facts.quote: River City is situated alongside the Chicago River and consists of two 7- to 14-story, serpentine residential towers constructed of reinforced, poured-in-place concrete "shells" with 449 residential units, varying in size from studios to 4-bedroom penthouses.

facts.fact: The towers sit on a four-storey post-and-beam plinth with commercial space, a health club, indoor parking and a 70-slip marina.
facts.quote: The towers sit on a 4-story post-and-beam "plinth" that contains approximately 225,000 square feet (20,900 m2) of commercial and office space, including a 50,000 sq ft (4,600 m2) health club with full-size pool, an underground, indoor parking lot, and a 70-slip marina with a bubbler system that prevents freezing and permits year-round use.

facts.fact: The plinth roof holds a one-acre private park and River Road, a 10-storey skylit atrium between the towers.
facts.quote: The roof of the base structure is a transfer floor that holds Skyline Park, a 1-acre, landscaped private park for the residents; as well as River Road, a 10-story, enclosed, skylighted atrium between the two residential towers.

facts.fact: It was first planned as a series of 72-storey skyscrapers in groups of three, joined every 18 storeys by triangular platforms.
facts.quote: It was to consist of a series of 72-story mixed-use skyscrapers, clustered in groups of three, and joined every 18 stories by triangular platforms containing resident services.

facts.fact: That plan was to house up to 30,000 families, the culmination of Goldberg's idea of a 'city within a city'.
facts.quote: The complex was intended to be capable of housing as many as 30,000 families, the grand culmination of Goldberg's utopian vision of a "city within a city".

facts.fact: Preservationists objected when the raw concrete of the River Road atrium was painted white.
facts.quote: Architectural preservationists complained when the raw concrete interior of the "River Road" atrium was painted white.

facts.fact: The guest house on East 52nd Street in Manhattan was designed by Philip Johnson and completed in 1950.
facts.quote: Situated on the southern sidewalk of 52nd Street between Second Avenue and Third Avenue, it was designed by Philip Johnson and completed in 1950.

facts.fact: It was built as a guest house for the philanthropist Blanchette Rockefeller, wife of John D. Rockefeller III.
facts.quote: The residence was constructed as a guest house for philanthropist Blanchette Rockefeller, who was married to John D. Rockefeller III.

facts.fact: It was the only private house Johnson designed in New York City.
facts.quote: It was the only private residence in New York City that Johnson designed.

facts.fact: Blanchette Rockefeller wanted a separate building for her modern art collection.
facts.quote: Johnson was hired to design the guest house in 1948 for Blanchette Rockefeller, who wanted a separate building to store her modern art collection, as her husband did not appreciate modern art.

facts.fact: The two-storey symmetrical facade is brick at ground level and glass above.
facts.quote: The two-story building contains a symmetrical facade of brick at ground level and glass above.

facts.fact: The upper storey is six translucent glass panels divided by four steel bars.
facts.quote: The second story is made of six translucent glass panels divided by four steel bars.

facts.fact: A garden with a pool separates the front living and dining room from the rear bedroom, each behind fully glazed walls.
facts.quote: These are separated by an outdoor garden with a pool, separated from either room by fully glazed walls.

facts.fact: The plan follows Mies van der Rohe's unbuilt 1930s court-house designs.
facts.quote: The interior arrangement was patterned after Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's unbuilt designs for "court houses" in the 1930s.

facts.fact: It became a New York City landmark in 2000.
facts.quote: The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the Rockefeller Guest House as an official landmark in 2000.

facts.fact: The Sciences Library ('SciLi') is a high-rise building at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island.
facts.quote: The Sciences Library (nicknamed "SciLi", pronounced “sigh-lie”) is a high-rise building at Brown University, located in Providence, Rhode Island, United States.

facts.fact: It was built in 1971 in the Brutalist style.
facts.quote: It was built in 1971 in the Brutalist style.

facts.fact: At 180 feet (55 m) it is among the tallest buildings in Providence.
facts.quote: At 180 feet (55 m), it is tied with One Citizens Plaza as the 16th-tallest building in the city.

facts.fact: The high-rise was Brown's answer to needing to expand with little land available in the late 1960s.
facts.quote: In the late 1960s, the school was faced with the desire for vigorous expansion but had little real estate available, and the high-rise library was the school's solution.

facts.fact: Warner Burns Toan & Lunde designed it, chiefly M. Rosaria Piomelli and Danforth Toan.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Warner Burns Toan & Lunde architects, primarily by M. Rosaria Piomelli and Danforth Toan.

facts.fact: It is one of four notable Brutalist buildings at Brown.
facts.quote: Along with the John D. Rockefeller Jr. Library (completed in 1964), the Graduate Center (completed in 1968), and the List Art Building (1971), it is one of four notable examples of brutalist architecture at Brown.

facts.fact: Architectural historian McKenzie Woodward criticised it for overwhelming everything around it.
facts.quote: Architectural historian McKenzie Woodward condemns the building as "overwhelm[ing] everything around it", even comparing it to a Soviet-era Panelák when viewed from its "all-too-many distant viewing perspectives".

facts.fact: In 2006 its lower floors were renovated into the Friedman Study Center.
facts.quote: In 2006, the first and second floors and the basement of the Sciences Library underwent extensive renovations and were transformed into the Susan P. and Richard A. Friedman Study Center.

facts.fact: Seventeenth Church of Christ, Scientist, built in 1968, is a modern Christian Science church at 55 East Wacker Drive in Chicago's Loop.
facts.quote: Seventeenth Church of Christ, Scientist, built in 1968, is a modern style Christian Science church building located in The Loop at 55 East Wacker Drive, (at Wabash Avenue) in Chicago, Illinois in the United States.

facts.fact: It was designed by the Chicago architect Harry Weese, best known for the Washington Metro.
facts.quote: It was designed by noted Chicago-based architect Harry Weese, whose most famous work is the Washington Metro but who is remembered best as the architect who "shaped Chicago’s skyline and the way the city thought about everything from the lakefront to its treasure-trove of historical buildings."

facts.fact: It is a circular concrete building with no ordinary windows in its amphitheatre.
facts.quote: Built by Sumner Sollitt Construction Company of concrete in a circular design, the building has no traditional windows in the interior amphitheater.

facts.fact: Daylight comes through a skylight at the top of the oculus in the centre of the conical roof.
facts.quote: Outside light comes through a skylight at the top of the oculus in the center of the conical roof.

facts.fact: Visitors enter by a bridge over a sunken garden, which lets light into the Sunday School below street level.
facts.quote: Pedestrian entrance to the building is via a bridge over a sunken garden, which Weese said "was for the benefit of the [subterranean] Sunday School, which didn't have any traditional windows" but is lit through the garden by the light from the street level above.

facts.fact: The semicircular auditorium seats 764, and no seat is more than 54 feet from the Readers' Platform.
facts.quote: The semicircular auditorium which seats 764 is designed so that no seat is more than 54 feet from the Readers' Platform, which is the focal point of all Christian Science church auditoriums.

facts.fact: In 1996 it received the 25 Year Award of the Chicago Chapter of the American Institute of Architects.
facts.quote: In 1996, Seventeenth Church received the 25 Year Award of the Chicago Chapter of the American Institute of Architects.

facts.fact: For the 2018 Illinois Bicentennial, AIA Illinois named it one of the Illinois 200 Great Places.
facts.quote: In celebration of the 2018 Illinois Bicentennial, the Seventeenth Church of Christ, Scientist was selected as one of the Illinois 200 Great Places by the American Institute of Architects Illinois component (AIA Illinois).

facts.fact: The Thomas Crane Public Library is a city library in Quincy, Massachusetts.
facts.quote: The Thomas Crane Public Library (TCPL) is a city library in Quincy, Massachusetts.

facts.fact: Known for its Richardsonian Romanesque architecture, it was paid for by the Crane family in memory of Thomas Crane, a stone contractor from the Quincy quarries.
facts.quote: Noted for its Richardsonian Romanesque architecture, the building was funded by the Crane family as a memorial to Thomas Crane, a wealthy stone contractor who got his start in the Quincy quarries.

facts.fact: It was built in four stages: Richardson's original (1882), a 1908 wing, a 1939 expansion and a 2001 addition that doubled its size.
facts.quote: The Thomas Crane Public Library was built in four stages: the original building (1882) by architect Henry Hobson Richardson; an additional ell with stack space and stained glass (1908) by William Martin Aiken in Richardson's style; a major expansion (1939) by architects Paul A. and Carroll Coletti, with stone carvings by sculptor Joseph Coletti of Quincy; and a recent addition (2001) by Boston architects Childs, Bertman, and Tseckares, which doubled the size of the library.

facts.fact: Richardson counted it among his most successful civic buildings, and Harper's Weekly called it 'the best village library in the United States'.
facts.quote: H. H. Richardson considered this library among his most successful civic buildings, and Harper's Weekly called it "the best village library in the United States".

facts.fact: It has a stained-glass window by John LaFarge in memory of Thomas Crane.
facts.quote: The building is host to a 30 × 10 inch stained-glass window by noted American artist John LaFarge in memory of Thomas Crane, Old Philosopher.

facts.fact: Frederick Law Olmsted designed the grounds.
facts.quote: The library's grounds were designed by renowned landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted, and renovated by the Olmsted Brothers between 1907 and 1911.

facts.fact: It ranked 43rd in the American Institute of Architects' 2007 poll of America's favourite buildings.
facts.quote: The library was ranked 43rd in a national poll conducted in 2007 by the American Institute of Architects of the favorite buildings in the nation.

facts.fact: It became a National Historic Landmark in 1987 as one of Richardson's finest libraries.
facts.quote: The Thomas Crane Public Library was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1987, recognizing it as one of Richardson's finest library buildings.

facts.fact: The church's sanctuary, designed by the local architect Charles M. Goodman in 1964, is a concrete Brutalist building listed on the National Register of Historic Places and the Virginia Landmarks Register in 2014.
facts.quote: UUCA's sanctuary building, designed by local architect Charles M. Goodman in 1964, is a concrete Brutalist structure that was listed on the National Register of Historic Places and Virginia Landmarks Register in 2014.

facts.fact: It is one of only three churches Goodman designed, and his only one in Virginia.
facts.quote: It is one of only three church buildings designed by Goodman and the only one in Virginia.

facts.fact: Founded in 1948, the congregation was the first Unitarian church in the Washington, D.C., suburbs.
facts.quote: Founded in 1948, UUCA was the first Unitarian church in Washington, D.C.'s suburbs.

facts.fact: Goodman's design included a sanctuary and an adjoining wing, which was not built at first because of the budget.
facts.quote: His design included plans for a main sanctuary and adjoining wing, the latter which was not built at the time due to budget concerns.

facts.fact: The sanctuary is a precast concrete building in the Brutalist style.
facts.quote: The sanctuary is a precast concrete building designed in the brutalist style.

facts.fact: It has an overhanging flat concrete roof and corrugated concrete wall panels.
facts.quote: It features an overhanging concrete flat roof, concrete block foundation, and corrugated concrete wall panels.

facts.fact: The meeting space is 62 feet square, with a polished reinforced concrete floor set in a large grid.
facts.quote: The sanctuary's meeting space measures 62 feet (19 m) by 62 feet and features a polished reinforced concrete floor set in a large grid pattern.

facts.fact: The sanctuary is designed for natural light, supplemented by patterned rows of light fixtures on the ceiling.
facts.quote: The sanctuary's design allows for the meeting space to have natural lighting which is complemented by patterned rows of light fixtures along the ceiling.

facts.fact: Later additions of 1994 and 2013 match the original in scale, style and materials and complete Goodman's plan to expand the church.
facts.quote: The two additions "complement the original building in their scale, style, material, and fenestration pattern, and fulfill Goodman’s original plans to expand the church with additional space for educational, administrative, and social functions."

facts.fact: The United States Tax Court Building, at 400 Second Street NW in Washington, D.C., is the headquarters of the US Tax Court.
facts.quote: The United States Tax Court Building is a courthouse located at 400 Second Street, Northwest, Washington, D.C., in the Judiciary Square neighborhood. It serves as the headquarters of the United States Tax Court.

facts.fact: Victor A. Lundy was chosen to design it in 1965.
facts.quote: Government officials selected architect Victor A. Lundy to design the building in 1965.

facts.fact: Lundy's 1966 concept had strong end masses, a central cantilevered courtroom block and a landscaped plaza.
facts.quote: In 1966, GSA approved Lundy's concept for a building with strong end masses, a central cantilevered courtroom block, and a landscaped plaza.

facts.fact: The building was dedicated on 22 November 1974, fifty years after the Revenue Act that created the court.
facts.quote: The completed building was dedicated on November 22, 1974, the fiftieth anniversary of the Revenue Act that created the court.

facts.fact: It reads as a cube broken into four parts: a cantilevered courtroom block at the front with office blocks to the sides and rear.
facts.quote: The building presents itself as a cube that has been deconstructed into four units: a dramatic cantilevered courtroom block on the front with office blocks on each side and to the rear.

facts.fact: It is clad in flame-treated Royal Pearl granite from Georgia and bronze-tinted glass with slim bronze aluminium mullions.
facts.quote: The building is clad in flame-treated Royal Pearl granite from Georgia and bronze-tinted, heat-absorbing, glare-reducing glass with slim bronze-anodized aluminum mullions.

facts.fact: Post-tensioned bridges, hidden steel cables and six slender columns hold up the 4,000-ton cantilevered courtroom block over the entrance.
facts.quote: Compression and post-tensioned bridges, steel cables hidden within the building's walls, and six slender columns together support the imposing 4,000-ton cantilevered courtroom block, which projects over the entrance.

facts.fact: Inside, a four-storey public hall, the Hall of Justice, is lit by a clerestory roof.
facts.quote: The interior is defined by a four-story central public hall, also called the Hall of Justice, crowned by a clerestory roof that admits light into the space.

facts.fact: The design won a GSA Honor Award in the first Design Awards Program in 1972.
facts.quote: Lundy's design won a GSA Honor Award in the first Design Awards Program held in 1972.

facts.fact: The Van Allen Building is a historic former department store in Clinton, Iowa.
facts.quote: The Van Allen Building, also known as Van Allen and Company Department Store, is a historic building at the northwest corner of Fifth Avenue South and Second Street in Clinton, Iowa, United States.

facts.fact: The four-storey building was designed by Louis Sullivan for John Delbert Van Allen.
facts.quote: The four-story building was designed by Louis Sullivan and commissioned by John Delbert Van Allen.

facts.fact: It was built as a department store between 1913 and 1914 and later converted to flats with shops.
facts.quote: Constructed between 1913 and 1914 as a department store, it has since been converted into an apartment building with commercial space.

facts.fact: Its steel frame resembles Sullivan's high-rise designs, and its facade is a scaled-down version of his Carson Pirie Scott Store in Chicago.
facts.quote: In particular, the steel frame is similar to Sullivan's high-rise designs, and the articulation (or arrangement) of the facade is a scaled-down version of the articulation used in Sullivan's earlier Carson Pirie Scott Store in Chicago.

facts.fact: Because the building is short and wide, Sullivan stressed the horizontal, with spandrel panels and wide windows.
facts.quote: Since the Van Allen Building was relatively short and wide, Sullivan articulated it horizontally, with horizontal spandrel panels and wide windows.

facts.fact: The upper floors are brick with terracotta ornament, including three decorative mullions.
facts.quote: The ground floor has storefront windows and entrances, while the upper stories have a brick facade with terracotta decorations such as three decorative mullions.

facts.fact: Unlike Sullivan's earlier work, the design includes some purely decorative elements, and the interior layout shaped the facade.
facts.quote: Unlike Sullivan's earlier work, the design includes some purely decorative elements, and the interior arrangement influenced the design of the facade.

facts.fact: It became a National Historic Landmark in January 1976, largely as one of the best-preserved examples of Sullivan's later work.
facts.quote: The Van Allen Building was designated as a National Historic Landmark in January 1976, in large part because it was one of the best-preserved surviving examples of Sullivan's later work.

facts.fact: The W. E. B. Du Bois Library is one of the libraries of the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
facts.quote: The W. E. B. Du Bois Library is one of the three libraries of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, Massachusetts, United States, the others being the Science and Engineering Library and the Wadsworth Library at the Charles River Campus (formerly Mount Ida Campus).

facts.fact: At 28 storeys and about 88 m tall, it is the third-tallest library in the world.
facts.quote: At 28 stories and 286 feet 4+1⁄8 inches (roughly 88 m) tall, it is the third-tallest library in the world after the National Library of Indonesia in Jakarta at 414 feet (126 m) and Shanghai Library in China at 348 feet (106 m).

facts.fact: It is considered the tallest academic research library in the world.
facts.quote: The W. E. B. Du Bois Library is also considered to be the tallest academic research library and 32nd tallest educational building in the world.

facts.fact: Edward Durell Stone designed it, following a consultant's advice that the university needed nearly 310,000 square feet.
facts.quote: The designer was Edward Durrell Stone who followed recommendations by a Boston library consultant who recommended that the university would require a building of nearly 310,000 square feet to meet with the growing demands of students.

facts.fact: Ground was broken in April 1969; it opened in 1973 and was dedicated in 1974.
facts.quote: Ground was broken in April 1969 and the building was opened to the public in 1973, with an official dedication taking place in 1974.

facts.fact: It was designed in units of three floors: two stack floors for related subjects and a carrel floor for the matching departments and librarians.
facts.quote: The building was designed to work in units of three, with two stacks floors holding similar subjects and a carrel floor to accommodate departments and librarians related to those materials.

facts.fact: It was closed in September 1979 because bits of brick were spalling from the facade.

facts.fact: In 1983 the state gave $2.5 million for a major renovation of the brick veneer.
facts.quote: In 1983, the university acquired $2.5 million from the state legislature to begin a major renovation of the building's brick veneer.

facts.fact: The W. R. Grace Building is a skyscraper in Manhattan, New York City.
facts.quote: The W. R. Grace Building is a skyscraper in Manhattan, New York City.

facts.fact: It was designed mainly by Gordon Bunshaft and completed in 1972.
facts.quote: The building was designed principally by Gordon Bunshaft, and completed in 1972.

facts.fact: It overlooks Bryant Park and the New York Public Library's main branch.
facts.quote: It overlooks Bryant Park and the New York Public Library's main branch.

facts.fact: It has 50 floors and is 630 feet (190 m) tall.

facts.fact: Its north and south facades slope in a concave curve.
facts.quote: One of the aesthetic attributes of the building is the concave vertical slope of its north and south facades, on 42nd and 43rd Street, though only the 42nd Street side has an entrance.

facts.fact: It uses Bunshaft's original, rejected facade design for the Solow Building.

facts.fact: It is clad in white travertine, contrasting with black windows.

facts.fact: Its unusual shape and the space taken by its plaza have drawn criticism since it opened.
facts.quote: The Grace building has faced backlash on its design since its opening in 1974, with many criticizing its addition to the skyline, the unusual shape, and question the space taken up by the surrounding plaza.

facts.fact: The Watergate complex is a group of six buildings in Foggy Bottom, Washington, D.C., with co-operative apartments, a hotel and an office building.
facts.quote: The Watergate complex is a group of six buildings in the Foggy Bottom neighborhood of Washington, D.C., United States. It includes a development of cooperative apartment residences, a hotel, and an office building.

facts.fact: Built between 1963 and 1971, it became one of the most desirable places to live in Washington.

facts.fact: The chief architect was Luigi Moretti of the University of Rome, with associate architect Milton Fischer of Corning, Moore, Elmore and Fischer.

facts.fact: It was the first mixed-use development in the District of Columbia.

facts.fact: It was meant as a 'city within a city' with so many amenities that residents would not need to leave.
facts.quote: The Watergate complex was intended to be a "city within a city", and provide so many amenities that residents would not need to leave.

facts.fact: Its curved buildings were designed to echo two nearby elements.

facts.fact: Because of its curves, it was one of the first major US building projects in which computers played a significant part in the design.

facts.fact: The curves also give residents views of the Potomac River.

facts.fact: The whole development was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 21 October 2005.
facts.quote: The entire development was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on October 21, 2005.

facts.fact: The Hallidie Building is an office building at 130 Sutter Street in San Francisco's Financial District.

facts.fact: It is known for its glass facade, symmetrical fire escapes and ornate ironwork.

facts.fact: The seven-storey building was preceded by Louis Curtiss's 1909 Boley Clothing Company building, and the Crystal Palace may have inspired Polk.

facts.fact: In 1971 San Francisco made it a historic monument when a bank considered replacing it.

facts.fact: A two-year restoration of its sheet-metal friezes, cornices, balconies and fire escapes was finished in April 2013.
facts.quote: The building underwent a two-year restoration, which was completed in April 2013, after its sheet metal friezes, cornices, balconies, and fire escapes were deemed unsafe by the City of San Francisco's Department of Building Inspection.

facts.fact: Horatio West Court, built in Santa Monica, California, in 1919, is an early example of attached houses with shared pedestrian and car access.
facts.quote: Horatio West Court, built in Santa Monica, California in 1919, is an early example of attached houses with shared pedestrian and vehicle access.

facts.fact: Its six small buildings, designed by Irving Gill, are grouped on a 60-foot lot.
facts.quote: The six little buildings are grouped on a 60-foot lot. It was designed by Irving Gill.

facts.fact: Two units sit on each side of a driveway leading to rear garages topped with small flats.
facts.quote: Horatio West Court divides its narrow lot symmetrically, placing two units on either side of a driveway that runs the length of the lot to a rear parking area, where two garages are topped with little apartments.

facts.fact: Each building is a flat-roofed two-storey cube with a small entrance porch and a walled terrace.
facts.quote: Each building is a slightly inflected, flat-roofed two-story cube to which a small entrance porch and a walled terrace has been added.

facts.fact: The arched entries and patios reflect Gill's liking for Mission Revival, but the buildings belong to the Modern Movement.
facts.quote: The arched entry ways and small patio courts reflect Gill's affinity for the Mission Revival style. However, the buildings themselves fall squarely into the Modern Movement.

facts.fact: Richard Neutra photographed it and published it in his 1930 book Amerika.
facts.quote: Richard Neutra extensively photographed the Horatio West Court as well as Gill's Dodge House and published in his book Amerika: Neues Bauen in der Welt (1930).

facts.fact: In 1977 it became the first building in Santa Monica listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
facts.quote: The Horatio West Court was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1977, the first building in the City of Santa Monica to be listed in the National Register.

facts.fact: Hyatt Regency San Francisco is a hotel at the foot of Market Street and The Embarcadero in San Francisco's financial district.
facts.quote: Hyatt Regency San Francisco is a hotel located at the foot of Market Street and The Embarcadero in the financial district of San Francisco, California.

facts.fact: It is part of the Embarcadero Center development by Trammell Crow, David Rockefeller and John Portman.
facts.quote: The hotel is a part of the Embarcadero Center development by Trammell Crow, David Rockefeller, and John Portman.

facts.fact: Its atrium holds the Guinness world record for the largest hotel lobby: 107 m long, 49 m wide and 52 m (15 storeys) high.
facts.quote: The atrium holds the Guinness world record (as of 2024) for the largest hotel lobby, with a length of 107 meters, width of 49 meters and height of 52 meters (15 stories).

facts.fact: Portman said the lobby design was suggested by the 1935 science-fiction film Things to Come.
facts.quote: Architect John Portman has stated that its design was suggested to him by viewing the 1935 science fiction film Things to Come.

facts.fact: The lobby holds Charles O. Perry's large modernist sculpture Eclipse.
facts.quote: The hotel has a large modernist sculpture Eclipse, by Charles O Perry that sits in the lobby.

facts.fact: Critic John King called the 1973 building a 'temple of hermetic urbanism', dated but still visually dazzling.
facts.quote: The San Francisco Chronicle's architecture critic John King has described the 1973 building as a "temple of hermetic urbanism" in a "self-contained sci-fi" style that by 2016 had become "dated", albeit remaining "still visually dazzling, in a futuristic sort of way."

facts.fact: Its atrium served as the Glass Tower lobby in the 1974 film The Towering Inferno.
facts.quote: The Hyatt Regency's atrium lobby served as the lobby of the Glass Tower in 1974's The Towering Inferno.

facts.fact: The Los Angeles County Hall of Records stands at the north end of the Civic Center in Downtown Los Angeles.
facts.quote: The Los Angeles County Hall of Records sits in the northern end of the Civic Center in Downtown Los Angeles.

facts.fact: The high-rise by Richard Neutra, co-designed with Robert Alexander, is an example of International Style architecture.
facts.quote: The high-rise building by Richard Neutra (co-designed by Robert Alexander) is an example of international style architecture.

facts.fact: Neutra and Alexander combined two planned buildings, one for records and one for workers, into one.
facts.quote: Originally envisioned as two separate buildings, one for storing records and the other for workers, Neutra and Alexander combined the buildings into one.

facts.fact: The T-shaped building has double-height floors with tall windows on the north and a records block with floors every 8 feet on the south.
facts.quote: The T-shaped building has odd number floors on the north side, with double high ceilings and tall windows. The records block on the south side, has floors at 8-ft intervals.

facts.fact: Large aluminium louvres run the full height of the south face to save energy.
facts.quote: The building was designed to be energy efficient, with large aluminum louvers on the south face running the height of the building.

facts.fact: The louvres originally turned with the sun during the day to let in more indirect light.
facts.quote: Originally, they turned with the angle of the sun throughout the day to allow more indirect light into the building.

facts.fact: Grilles and screens by Malcolm Leland flank the escalators.
facts.quote: The escalators from the ground through 3rd floor are flanked by grilles and screens designed by Malcolm Leland, also known for his work in the ModulArt movement.

facts.fact: It was nominated for the AIA's 1964 R. S. Reynolds Memorial Award.
facts.quote: The building was nominated for the 1964 R. S. Reynolds Memorial Award by the American Institute of Architects.

facts.fact: The Mark Taper Forum is a 739-seat thrust-stage theatre at the Los Angeles Music Center, designed by Welton Becket and Associates on Bunker Hill.
facts.quote: The Mark Taper Forum is a 739-seat thrust stage at the Los Angeles Music Center designed by Welton Becket and Associates on the Bunker Hill section of downtown Los Angeles.

facts.fact: It opened in 1967 as part of the Los Angeles Music Center.
facts.quote: The Mark Taper Forum opened in 1967 as part of the Los Angeles Music Center, the West Coast equivalent of Lincoln Center, designed by Los Angeles architect Welton Becket and Associates.

facts.fact: Becket designed the centre in the New Formalism style, which stressed geometric shapes.
facts.quote: Becket designed the center in the style of New Formalism, which emphasized geometric shapes.

facts.fact: The perfectly circular Taper, wrapped in a lacy precast relief by Jacques Overhoff, is considered one of Becket's best works.
facts.quote: The perfectly circular Taper is considered one of his best works, featuring a distinctive decorated drum of a design with its exterior wrapped in a lacy precast relief by Jacques Overhoff.

facts.fact: The lobby has a curving abalone wall by Tony Duquette.
facts.quote: The lobby has a curving, abalone wall by Tony Duquette.

facts.fact: Its thrust stage juts into a semicircular amphitheatre, creating an intimate link between audience and performers.
facts.quote: The Taper became known for its thrust stage, jutting into a classical, semicircular amphitheater, which creates an especially intimate relationship between audience and performer.

facts.fact: Becket designed the building without knowing who would use it.
facts.quote: Becket designed the building not knowing who would use it.

facts.fact: A $30 million renovation by Rios Clementi Hale Studios began in July 2007.
facts.quote: A $30-million renovation of the Taper led by the Los Angeles firm Rios Clementi Hale Studios began in July 2007 after the 2006/2007 season.

facts.fact: The renovation updated almost everything that was not concrete while keeping the circular shape.
facts.quote: The renovation updated nearly everything that was not concrete and did not disrupt the building's circular shape.

facts.fact: The Pacific Design Center is a 1,600,000-square-foot complex for the design community in West Hollywood, California.
facts.quote: The Pacific Design Center, or PDC, is a 1,600,000-square-foot (150,000 m2) multi-use facility for the design community in West Hollywood, California.

facts.fact: One building is nicknamed the Blue Whale for its size relative to its neighbours and its bright blue glass cladding.
facts.quote: One of the buildings is often described as the Blue Whale because of its large size relative to surrounding buildings and its brilliant blue glass cladding.

facts.fact: Designed by the Argentine architect César Pelli, the 14-acre campus opened in 1975 with the 750,000-square-foot Center Blue.
facts.quote: Designed by Argentine architect César Pelli, the 14-acre (57,000 m2) campus opened in 1975, with the 750,000-square-foot (70,000 m2) Center Blue.

facts.fact: Architect Norma Merrick Sklarek also contributed to the design.
facts.quote: Architect Norma Merrick Sklarek also contributed to the architectural design of the building.

facts.fact: It was Pelli's first landmark building.
facts.quote: Pelli designed his first landmark building with the Pacific Design Center in West Hollywood, California, which was completed 1975 and became known by the locals as the "Blue Whale".

facts.fact: Center Green opened in 1988, adding 450,000 square feet.
facts.quote: Center Green opened in 1988, adding 450,000 square feet (42,000 m2).

facts.fact: The final phase, Center Red, opened in 2013.
facts.quote: The final phase of the plan, Center Red, opened in 2013 with an additional 400,000 square feet (37,000 m2).

facts.fact: Pelli designed the three-building complex while at Gruen Associates.
facts.quote: In 2012, the three-building Pacific Design Center, which Pelli designed 40 years earlier while at Gruen Associates, was completed with the addition of the Red Building.

facts.fact: It has 100 showrooms selling interior products to designers, architects and decorators.
facts.quote: The Center has 100 showrooms which display and sell 2,200 interior product lines to professional interior designers, architects, facility managers, decorators and dealers.

facts.fact: Parker Center was the headquarters of the Los Angeles Police Department from 1955 until October 2009.
facts.quote: Parker Center, initially named the Police Administration Building or Police Facilities Building, was the former headquarters of the Los Angeles Police Department from 1955 until October 2009.

facts.fact: Groundbreaking was on 30 December 1952 and construction was completed in 1955.
facts.quote: Groundbreaking for the center began on December 30, 1952, and construction was completed in 1955.

facts.fact: The architects were Welton Becket & Associates, with J. E. Stanton as associated architect.
facts.quote: The architect was Welton Becket & Associates and J.E. Stanton, associated architect.

facts.fact: Maynard Woodard was director of design and Francis Runcy project architect.
facts.quote: Maynard Woodard was director of design and Francis Runcy was the project architect.

facts.fact: The eight-storey building was reinforced concrete with aluminium sash windows covered by louvres.
facts.quote: The eight-story building was of reinforced concrete with aluminum sash windows covered by louvers.

facts.fact: Gladding, McBean ceramic tile covered the west elevation.
facts.quote: Ceramic tile by Gladding, McBean covered the west elevation.

facts.fact: It brought together police facilities spread across the Civic Center area.
facts.quote: The building combined police facilities that had been located throughout the Civic Center area.

facts.fact: Two artworks were commissioned: Bernard Rosenthal's bronze sculpture The American Family at the entrance and Joseph Young's mosaic of Los Angeles landmarks in the lobby.
facts.quote: Two prominent artworks were commissioned for the building, a large bronze modernist sculpture by Bernard Rosenthal mounted at the entrance titled "The American Family" and a mosaic work in the lobby depicting architectural landmarks of Los Angeles by Joseph Young.

facts.fact: Its above-ground demolition was completed on 15 July 2019.
facts.quote: The above-ground demolition of Parker Center was completed on July 15, 2019. == In popular culture == Parker Center appears in the police procedural media franchise Dragnet, beginning with the fifth season of the 1955 television series.

facts.fact: The Pearlman Mountain Cabin is a cottage in Idyllwild, California.
facts.quote: The Pearlman Mountain Cabin is a cottage in Idyllwild, United States.

facts.fact: John Lautner designed it in 1957.
facts.quote: It was designed by John Lautner in 1957.

facts.fact: It is on the National Register of Historic Places as 'character-defining' of organic architecture.
facts.quote: It is listed in the National Register of Historic Places as "character-defining" for the architectural style of organic architecture.

facts.fact: The lot was difficult: it sloped up to 40% and was full of rocks.
facts.quote: The Pearlmans had purchased a lot that was considered to be fraught with problems: It had a slope of up to 40% and was full of rocks.

facts.fact: Lautner built a circular platform over a large boulder and made the cabin a cylinder, its flat overhanging roof held up by tree trunks around it.
facts.quote: Lautner decided to overbuild the boulder with a circular platform and to construct the cabin as a cylinder, its flat, overhanging roof being supported by tree trunks encircling the cabin.

facts.fact: Apart from the tree trunks, the living room's outer wall is all glass, set in a zigzag that roughly forms a semicircle.
facts.quote: Apart from the supporting tree trunks, its outer wall completely consists of glass windows that form a zigzag line roughly resembling a semi-circle.

facts.fact: The large, unusually arranged windows blur the line between inside and outside.
facts.quote: Because of the large size and the unusual collocation of the windows the boundaries between inside and outside become blurred for the viewer.

facts.fact: Roof and facade were designed for good acoustics because Agnes Pearlman was a talented pianist.
facts.quote: Roof and facade have been designed to provide good acoustics inside, the trigger being that Agnes Pearlman was a talented pianist.
